**Primate city** (Kolkata, Chennai in their regions), **rank-size rule**, **conurbation** (Delhi NCR), **million-plus cities: 53 in 2011, projected 68-70 by 2031**, **census towns**, **peri-urban interface**, **urban heat island** (Delhi's core runs several degrees above its periphery), and **urban flooding** — Chennai 2015, Mumbai 2005 and 2021, Bengaluru 2022 — caused by encroached wetlands and stormwater drains, addressed by the **NDMA Urban Flooding Guidelines (2010)**, the first of their kind in the world.

sections.h: Judgments, Statutes and Schemes for GS-1

groups.g: Judgments a society answer can carry

items.d: A **daughter is a coparcener by birth** under the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act — the right is unobstructed heritage, so it applies whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005. The single best citation for women's land and property rights.

*Shayara Bano* struck down **instant triple talaq** as manifestly arbitrary (codified in the 2019 Act); *Shah Bano* granted maintenance under **Section 125 CrPC**, was reversed by the 1986 Act, and then substantially restored by *Danial Latifi* (2001). Together they are the standing example of the **personal law versus gender justice** conflict.

*Lata Singh* — an adult woman is free to marry whom she chooses, and **inter-caste marriage deserves state protection, not harassment**. *Shakti Vahini* — laid down preventive, remedial and punitive measures against **honour killings and khap panchayats**, holding that **'the consent of the family, community or clan is not necessary'** for a marriage between two consenting adults.

*Shirur Mutt* created the **essential religious practices** doctrine; *Sabarimala* held the exclusion of women aged 10-50 was not essential and violated Articles 14, 15, 17, 21 and 25, holding that **constitutional morality prevails over social morality** — with Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent on the limits of judicial review of faith. Pending before a nine-judge bench.

items.t: Suchita Srivastava (2009) and the MTP amendments
items.d: **Reproductive choice is part of personal liberty under Article 21** — a woman's right to make reproductive decisions cannot be overridden without her consent. The **MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021** extended the limit to **24 weeks** for specified categories, allowed unmarried women's access (by replacing 'husband' with 'partner'), and created **Medical Boards** for foetal-abnormality cases beyond 24 weeks.

*NALSA* recognised **transgender persons as a third gender** with a right to **self-identification**; *Navtej Johar* decriminalised consensual same-sex relations. *Supriyo* (2023) declined to recognise same-sex marriage, leaving it to Parliament while directing a **committee on the rights of queer couples** — the current position.

*Indra Sawhney* — caste can be a starting point for identifying a backward class, the **creamy layer** must be excluded, and reservation is capped at **50%** save in extraordinary circumstances. *Davinder Singh* (2024) permitted **sub-classification within Scheduled Castes**, overruling *E.V. Chinnaiah* — the key development for the 'heterogeneity within backwardness' argument.

items.t: Aligarh Muslim University (2024) and T.M.A. Pai (2002)
items.d: *AMU* overruled *Azeez Basha*: an institution created by statute can still be a minority institution — the test is **who founded it and for whose benefit**. *T.M.A. Pai* fixed the **state as the unit** for minority status and secured the autonomy of unaided institutions. Read with **Articles 29 and 30**.

groups.g: Statutes and schemes for society answers

items.d: **Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961**; **PCPNDT Act, 1994** (prohibits sex determination, not sex selection alone); **Domestic Violence Act, 2005** — civil remedies, residence orders, protection officers; **POSH Act, 2013** from *Vishaka*; **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013** from the Verma Committee; **Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019**; **Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021** and the **ART Act, 2021** — altruistic surrogacy only, with a national registry; **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006**, with the **age-raising bill to 21** pending.

**JJ Act, 2015** — permits trying 16-18 year olds as adults for heinous offences after a Juvenile Justice Board assessment; **POCSO, 2012** — gender-neutral, presumption of guilt, child-friendly procedure, special courts; **Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016** — bans employment below 14 entirely and 14-18 in hazardous occupations, but permits **'family enterprise'** work, the standing criticism; **Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976**; **Trafficking of Persons Bill** still pending.

**Beti Bachao Beti Padhao**, **Sukanya Samriddhi**, **Mission Shakti (Sambal and Samarthya)**, **PM-AJAY** and **SHRESHTA** for SC students, **Eklavya Model Residential Schools (728 sanctioned)** for tribal children, **PM-JANMAN (₹24,104 crore for 75 PVTGs)**, **DAJGUA (₹79,156 crore, 63,000 tribal villages)**, **NAMASTE** for sanitation workers, **SMILE** for beggary and transgender persons, and **Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana** for the elderly.

**AMASR Act, 1958 (amended 2010)** — prohibited area 100 m and regulated area 200 m around a protected monument, with the **National Monuments Authority**; ASI protects **3,698 monuments** while thousands more are unprotected or state-listed; the **National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities**; **Adopt a Heritage / Monument Mitra**; the **National Mission for Manuscripts (2003)** — over 5 million manuscripts, the world's largest collection; **PRASHAD** and **Swadesh Darshan 2.0** for pilgrimage and thematic circuits.

**Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule's school for girls (1848)** and the Satyashodhak Samaj; a century later, **Kerala's near-universal literacy** built on the Travancore-Cochin missionary and princely investment plus the **1957 land reforms**. *Lesson: caste hierarchy weakens fastest where education and land redistribution act together — either alone produces mobility without structural change (Srinivas's Sanskritisation).*

**Kudumbashree (Kerala, 46 lakh women)** and **SEWA (Ela Bhatt, Ahmedabad, 1972 — organising self-employed women, now 2.5 million members and a cooperative bank)**. *Lesson: for informal women workers, the union and the cooperative do what labour law cannot — they create the counterparty that the law assumes already exists.*

**Sati abolition (1829)** — Rammohan Roy's scriptural argument plus Bentinck's law; **Devadasi abolition**; **Kerala and Tamil Nadu's temple-entry proclamations (1936, 1939)**; and against these, the **persistence of manual scavenging** despite the 1993 and 2013 Acts. *Lesson: a practice ends when law, social reform from within the tradition, and an alternative livelihood arrive together — the third element is what manual scavenging still lacks.*

**Linguistic reorganisation (1956)** defused the language question that Selig Harrison called India's 'most dangerous decade'; the **Sixth Schedule councils** and the **Bodo, Karbi Anglong and ULFA accords** did the same for ethnic autonomy. *Lesson: India accommodates identity through asymmetric federalism rather than suppressing it — accommodation converts secession into representation.*

The **Justice Sachar Committee (2006)** found Muslims below the national average on most indicators; **Justice Srikrishna (Mumbai, 1993)** and **Justice Nanavati** inquiries; and the **communal-violence response of the Kerala and Bhiwandi (mohalla committees, Suresh Khopde)** models, where police-community committees pre-empted riots. *Lesson: prevention is local and institutional — a mohalla committee is worth more than a post-riot commission.*

**Chennai (2015)** — the Adyar and Cooum floodplains and 300+ waterbodies encroached; **Mumbai (2005, 2021)** — the Mithi river narrowed and mangroves cleared; **Bengaluru (2022)** — lakes and rajakaluves built over. *Lesson: urban flooding is a land-use failure, not a rainfall event — the NDMA's Urban Flooding Guidelines (2010, the world's first) exist and are ignored at the master-plan stage.*

**Chennai's 'Day Zero' (2019)** and the recovery through **mandatory rooftop rainwater harvesting (a 2003 amendment to the building rules)** and restored eris (tank irrigation systems). *Lesson: the traditional tank cascade was the city's original water system — restoration beat augmentation.*

**Ahmedabad — India's first UNESCO World Heritage City (2017)** with its pols and heritage walk; **Hampi and Khajuraho** as tourism economies; and **Maratha Military Landscapes (2025)** as the newest inscription. *Lesson: inscription is a conservation obligation and a livelihood asset simultaneously — the risk is over-tourism, as at Venice and increasingly at Ladakh and Manali.*

**Kerala's response to inter-state migrant workers** — the **Awaz health insurance scheme, Apna Ghar hostels and Roshni** schooling for migrant children, and the deliberate official term **'guest workers'**. Against it, the 2020 exodus that followed the national lockdown. *Lesson: a receiving state that registers, insures and schools migrants converts an invisible workforce into a governed one — one nation one ration card is the national version of the same insight.*

**Joshimath subsidence (2023)** — the **Mishra Committee had warned in 1976** that the town sits on old landslide debris and construction should be restricted; **Wayanad landslides (2024)** in a zone the **Gadgil report** classified ESZ-1. *Lesson: in both cases the science existed decades earlier — the failure is not of knowledge but of the land-use decision that overrode it.*
Gandhi's first satyagraha in India — against the **tinkathia system** forcing indigo cultivation on 3/20th of holdings; Rajkumar Shukla brought him. Outcome: the Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918.
Revenue-remission satyagraha after crop failure; **Sardar Patel and Indulal Yagnik** joined Gandhi. Established the tactic of **no-tax campaigns**.
Gandhi's **first hunger strike**, over a plague bonus dispute; produced the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association and the doctrine of arbitration between capital and labour.

'**No dakeel, no vakeel, no appeal**' — detention without trial; provoked the first all-India hartal and, on 13 April, **Jallianwala Bagh** (General Dyer; the Hunter Commission; Tagore renounced his knighthood).

Boycott of councils, courts, schools and foreign cloth; merged with the **Khilafat** movement — the high point of Hindu-Muslim unity. Withdrawn after **Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922)**, which C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru opposed, leading to the **Swaraj Party (1923)**.
All-white statutory commission — 'Simon Go Back'; **Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in the Lahore lathi charge** and died. Its report fed into the Government of India Act, 1935.

The first Indian-drafted constitution — **dominion status**, a bill of rights, joint electorates with reservation for minorities where they were in a minority, and a federal structure. Jinnah responded with the **Fourteen Points (1929)**.
Nehru presiding — **Purna Swaraj** adopted; **26 January 1930** observed as Independence Day, the date later chosen for the Constitution's commencement.

**12 March-6 April, 385 km, 78 satyagrahis** from Sabarmati to Dandi, breaking the salt law; **Dharasana** (Sarojini Naidu, after Gandhi's arrest) drew global attention through Webb Miller's reporting.

**First** — Congress absent; **Second** — Gandhi attended alone after the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)**, deadlocked over minorities; **Third** — Congress absent. Followed by the **Communal Award (1932)** and the **Poona Pact**.

Gandhi's fast unto death against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes; Ambedkar agreed to **reserved seats within joint electorates** — raised from 71 to **148**. The compromise that shaped India's reservation architecture.

**Provincial autonomy** replacing dyarchy at the province and introducing it at the Centre, a federation that never came into being, a Federal Court (1937), the **RBI**, and separate electorates extended. Roughly **250 of the Constitution's provisions** derive from it.

**August Offer** — dominion status after the war, an expanded Executive Council, a war advisory council; rejected. **Cripps** — dominion status with a constituent assembly and the right of provinces to stay out; Gandhi called it '**a post-dated cheque on a crashing bank**'.

'**Do or Die**' (8 August, Bombay); the entire leadership arrested within hours, and the movement became **spontaneous and decentralised** — parallel governments at **Ballia, Tamluk (Midnapore) and Satara** were its most striking feature.

**Azad Hind Government proclaimed 21 October 1943**; the **Red Fort trials of Shah Nawaz Khan, P.K. Sahgal and G.S. Dhillon** — deliberately one Muslim, one Hindu and one Sikh — produced a wave of nationalist feeling that, with the **Royal Indian Navy mutiny (February 1946)**, convinced Britain the loyalty of the armed forces could no longer be assumed.

Rejected Pakistan, proposed a **three-tier federation with grouping of provinces** and a Constituent Assembly elected by provincial assemblies; the interpretation of grouping broke the plan. **Direct Action Day (16 August 1946)** followed.

**3 June Plan**; the **Indian Independence Act (18 July)**; the **Radcliffe Line** drawn in five weeks by a man who had never visited India; 10-12 million displaced and up to a million killed — the largest forced migration in history.

First sat **9 December 1946**; **Sachchidananda Sinha** provisional and **Rajendra Prasad** permanent president; **Ambedkar** chaired the Drafting Committee (7 members); **B.N. Rau** as constitutional adviser. Took **2 years 11 months 18 days**, held 11 sessions, and adopted the Constitution on **26 November 1949**, in force **26 January 1950**.

groups.g: Society, culture and geography — rapid terms

items.d: **M.N. Srinivas** — a lower caste adopts the ritual and lifestyle of a higher one to claim mobility; **positional, not structural, change**.
**Srinivas** — numerical preponderance, economic and political power, and a not-too-low ritual status; the caste that controls a village's land and votes.

The declining influence of religion over public institutions; in India it coexists with **increasing religiosity in private life** — which is why 'secularisation' and 'secularism' must be distinguished in an answer.
**Ogburn** — material culture changes faster than non-material culture (values, norms); explains why technology diffuses in rural India faster than the attitudes that would make it emancipatory.

**Putnam** — bonding (within a group) versus bridging (across groups); India's high bonding and low bridging capital is a standard explanation for why caste networks deliver but civic institutions underperform.

items.t: Feminisation of agriculture and of ageing
items.d: **Agriculture** — men migrate out, women become the de facto cultivators (~63% of the agricultural workforce) without land title. **Ageing** — women outlive men, so the elderly poor are disproportionately widowed women.

The growth advantage of a rising working-age share — India's window runs to about **2055**, peaking in the 2030s, and is **state-asymmetric**: already closing in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, still opening in Bihar and UP.

**Lee's** model of push, pull, intervening obstacles and personal factors; **Ravenstein's laws**; and **Todaro's** insight that migration responds to *expected* urban income, which is why urban unemployment does not stop rural-urban flows.

**Glocalisation** (Robertson), **cultural homogenisation versus hybridisation**, **McDonaldisation (Ritzer — efficiency, calculability, predictability, control)**, and the **'cultural lag' of consumption outrunning income**. Indian instance: the persistence of arranged marriage inside a globalised economy.

**Absolute versus relative**; **income versus multidimensional**; the **poverty line committees — Lakdawala (1993), Tendulkar (2009, 21.9% in 2011-12) and Rangarajan (2014, 29.5%)**; and the **poverty trap**. India has had **no official poverty line since 2011-12** — NITI's MPI is the working substitute.

items.t: Inversion of the sex ratio problem
items.d: The **child sex ratio (0-6) has been falling even as the overall ratio improves** — because sex-selective abortion tracks prosperity and small family size, not poverty. Haryana and Punjab, among the richest states, have the worst ratios: the standard counter-intuitive point.

Agriculture's share of GVA is ~18%, but **a monsoon failure still moves headline inflation and rural demand** because 46% of employment and most of the rural wage economy depend on it — output share understates macro significance.

Lines joining equal **rainfall, temperature, pressure and salinity**. India's **100 cm isohyet** roughly separates rice from wheat country, and the **50 cm isohyet** marks the boundary of assured rainfed agriculture.

The **Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet** must withdraw north of the Himalaya for the monsoon to burst; the **Tropical Easterly Jet** over peninsular India strengthens it; and **Western Disturbances** embedded in the westerly jet bring the winter rain the rabi crop depends on.

items.t: El Niño, La Niña and IOD
items.d: **El Niño** (warm eastern Pacific) suppresses the Indian monsoon; **La Niña** strengthens it; a **positive Indian Ocean Dipole** (warm west, cool east Indian Ocean) can offset an El Niño — which is why 'El Niño year = drought' is too crude for a good answer.

**Temperature inversion** in winter traps pollutants near the surface — the mechanism behind Delhi's winter smog and the Kashmir valley's frost. A **radiation inversion** on clear calm nights is the common form.

The northern plain's four belts — **Bhabar** (porous pebbly, streams disappear), **Terai** (marshy, re-emergent water, once malarial forest), **Bhangar** (older alluvium with kankar), **Khadar** (newer alluvium, annually renewed, most fertile).

**Regur/black cotton** — Deccan lava, moisture-retentive, self-ploughing, high in lime and potash, poor in nitrogen. **Laterite** — heavy rain and leaching, poor in humus, used as building brick. **Alluvial** — ~40% of India's area, the basis of the Indo-Gangetic plain's density.

sections.h: Rapid Recall — Culture, Texts and Monuments

groups.g: One line each — art and architecture

items.d: Ashokan brick core, enlarged in stone under the **Sungas**, four **toranas** carved under the **Satavahanas**; UNESCO site. Buddha depicted **aniconically** here.

**Rajaraja I, c. 1010**, Chola; 60 m vimana; one of the 'Great Living Chola Temples' (with Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Airavatesvara); its inscriptions are a complete record of temple endowments and administration.
**Rashtrakuta, 8th century**, Cave 16 — monolithic, carved **top-down from living rock**, the largest such excavation in the world.
**Narasimhadeva I, 13th century, Eastern Ganga** — conceived as Surya's chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses; Odisha (Kalinga) idiom of the Nagara style.
**Solanki, 1026**, Gujarat — the **surya kund** stepped tank, and a sanctum aligned so the equinox sun strikes the image.
**Chandella, 10th-11th century** — panchayatana plan, clustered shikharas rising like a mountain range, and sculpture organised in horizontal bands. UNESCO site.
**Belur, Halebid, Somnathpur** — soapstone, **stellate plan**, lathe-turned pillars, jagati platform; inscribed by UNESCO in **2023** as the 'Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas'.
**Pallava, 7th-8th century** — monolithic rathas, the Shore Temple, and 'Descent of the Ganga/Arjuna's Penance', the largest open-air rock relief in the world.
**Ajanta** — 29 caves, **Buddhist only**, famous for **murals in tempera on mud plaster**; **Ellora** — 34 caves, **Buddhist, Hindu and Jain together**, famous for sculpture and the Kailasanatha.

**Gandhara** — Greco-Roman, grey schist, wavy hair, realistic drapery; **Mathura** — indigenous, spotted red sandstone, energetic and fleshy; **Amaravati** — white marble, narrative medallions, slender and dynamic figures.
**Qutb Minar and Quwwat-ul-Islam (Slave dynasty)** — corbelled arches and reused temple pillars; the **Alai Darwaza (Khalji, 1311)** introduced the **true arch and true dome**.
**Bijapur, Adil Shahi, 1656** — the second largest dome in the world unsupported by pillars, with the **whispering gallery**; the peak of Deccan provincial style.

**Humayun's Tomb (1570)** — the **first garden tomb** in India and the prototype of the **charbagh** layout; the **Taj Mahal (1632-53)** perfected it with white marble, **pietra dura** inlay and complete bilateral symmetry, set on a riverfront terrace.
**Akbar's capital (1571-85)** — the Buland Darwaza, Diwan-i-Khas with its central pillar, Panch Mahal and Jodha Bai's palace; a synthesis of Gujarati, Bengali and Persian idioms in red sandstone.

items.t: Indian Ocean trade and temple towns
items.d: **Muziris, Arikamedu, Tamralipti, Bharuch (Barygaza)** as ancient ports; the **Periplus of the Erythraean Sea** as the source; and temple towns (Kanchi, Madurai, Thanjavur) as centres of production, banking and land management, not merely worship.

**Eleven now** — Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014), and **Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (2024)**. Criteria: high antiquity of early texts, a valuable body of ancient literature, an original literary tradition, and a distinct classical form.

**c. 300 BCE-300 CE**, Tamil — *Tolkappiyam* (grammar), *Ettuthogai* (eight anthologies), *Pattuppattu* (ten idylls), and the twin epics *Silappadikaram* and *Manimekalai*. Divided thematically into **akam** (interior/love) and **puram** (exterior/war and public life), with the **five tinai** landscapes.

**Buddhist councils** — Rajgriha (483 BCE), Vaishali (383), **Pataliputra under Ashoka (250)**, and **Kashmir under Kanishka (72 CE)**, where the Mahayana-Hinayana split hardened. **Jain councils** — Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE) and **Valabhi (512 CE)**, where the Agamas were compiled; the Digambara-Svetambara split preceded them.

**Major Rock Edicts (14), Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts (7), Cave inscriptions (Barabar)**; **Rock Edict XIII** describes the Kalinga war and remorse; **Rock Edict XII** is the classic statement of religious tolerance ('honour another's sect'). Languages: Prakrit in Brahmi and Kharosthi, plus **Greek and Aramaic** at Kandahar.

The **Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c. 920 CE)** record the **kudavolai** system — election by lot to village committees (variyams), with qualifications and disqualifications for candidates. India's oldest documented electoral procedure and a standing value addition for local-governance answers.

Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty, Equality, Fraternity — dignity of the individual and unity and **integrity** of the nation. 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' were inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**. Held to be **part of the Constitution and amendable but not its basic structure** in *Kesavananda* and reaffirmed in 2024.

India, that is Bharat, shall be a **Union of States** — Ambedkar: the Union is not the result of an agreement among states and no state has the **right to secede**. The textual anchor for 'indestructible union of destructible states'.

Art. 2 admits or establishes **new** states; **Art. 3** forms new states and alters areas, boundaries or names of existing states — needs the **President's recommendation** and reference to the state legislature **whose view is not binding**. Basis of linguistic reorganisation and of Telangana (2014) and the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019.

Citizenship at commencement; **Art. 11** empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law — hence the **Citizenship Act, 1955** and its amendments (1986, 2003 introducing the NRC/NPR framework, and 2019). Citizenship is a **Union subject (List I, Entry 17)**.

Definition of **'State'** — includes Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, **local authorities and 'other authorities'**. 'Other authorities' extended to instrumentalities of the state by the six-fold test in *Ajay Hasia* and *R.D. Shetty*; BCCI held amenable to writ jurisdiction for public functions.

Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are **void** — the textual basis of **judicial review**. Carries the doctrines of **severability**, **eclipse**, and **waiver is not permitted** (a citizen cannot waive a fundamental right — *Basheshar Nath*). **Art. 13(4)** excludes constitutional amendments, which is why *Kesavananda* had to build basic structure.

Equality before law (Dicey's negative concept) and equal protection of the laws (positive). Tests: **reasonable classification** (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) and, since *E.P. Royappa*, the **arbitrariness test** — 'equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies'. Extended to **manifest arbitrariness** of legislation in *Shayara Bano*.

15(1) bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; **15(3)** special provisions for women and children; **15(4)** SEBC/SC/ST advancement; **15(5)** private unaided institutions (93rd Amendment); **15(6)** and **16(6)** EWS 10% (103rd Amendment, upheld in *Janhit Abhiyan* 2022). 16(4) reservation in appointments; **16(4A)** promotion with consequential seniority; **16(4B)** carry-forward of backlog vacancies.

**Abolition of untouchability** — the only fundamental right enforceable against private individuals as well; operationalised through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989**. Invoked in *Sabarimala* by Chandrachud J. to cover exclusion based on notions of purity and pollution.

**19(1)(a)-(g)** six freedoms, each with its own reasonableness clause (19(2)-(6)); **Art. 21** life and personal liberty, transformed by *Maneka Gandhi* into a **'procedure established by law' that must be just, fair and reasonable** — importing substantive due process. The **golden triangle is Articles 14, 19 and 21** (*Minerva Mills*).

Read into Art. 21: **privacy** (*Puttaswamy* 2017), **clean environment** (*Subhash Kumar*), **livelihood** (*Olga Tellis*), **speedy trial** (*Hussainara Khatoon*), **legal aid** (*M.H. Hoskot*), **shelter**, **health**, **dignity**, **against a clean environment free of climate impacts** (*M.K. Ranjitsinh* 2024), **passive euthanasia and living wills** (*Common Cause* 2018), and the **right to be forgotten** in emerging jurisprudence. Naming three with case-tags is worth more than listing ten.

**86th Amendment, 2002** made free and compulsory education for **6-14 years** a fundamental right (Art. 21A), moved the earlier Art. 45 directive to **early childhood care and education below 6**, and added the parental duty under **Art. 51A(k)**. Implemented by the **RTE Act, 2009**, upheld in *Society for Unaided Private Schools* (2012).

Protection against arrest and detention — right to be informed of grounds, to consult counsel, and production before a magistrate within **24 hours**; **but 22(3)** excludes enemy aliens and **preventive detention**. 22(4)-(7) permit detention up to **3 months** without an Advisory Board. India is the only major democracy with **peacetime preventive detention in the Constitution itself**.

**23** prohibits traffic in human beings and **begar/forced labour** — the basis of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 and of *PUDR v. Union of India* (1982), which held that **payment below minimum wage is forced labour**. **24** bars employment of children under 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.

**25** freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, subject to public order, morality, health and **the state's power to make social welfare and reform laws**; **26** rights of religious denominations; **27** no compulsion to pay taxes for promotion of a religion; **28** religious instruction in state-funded institutions. The **essential religious practices doctrine** comes from *Shirur Mutt* (1954).

**29** protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens; **30** gives **minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions**, and 30(1A) requires that compensation on acquisition not defeat that right. *T.M.A. Pai* (2002) fixed the **state as the unit** for determining minority status; *Aligarh Muslim University* (2024) overruled *Azeez Basha* and laid down the **indicia test** for minority character.

Right to constitutional remedies — Ambedkar's **"heart and soul of the Constitution"**. Five writs: **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto**. Art. 32 is itself a fundamental right and **cannot be suspended except under Art. 359** during an emergency; the SC's power under 32 is part of the **basic structure**.

The **44th Amendment, 1978** deleted the right to property from Part III and made it a **constitutional right under Article 300A** ('no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law'). *Minerva Mills* struck down the extension of Art. 31C protection to all DPSPs, restoring the balance between Parts III and IV.

**39(b)-(c)** material resources and concentration of wealth; **39A** equal justice and free legal aid (42nd Amendment); **40** organisation of village panchayats; **41** right to work, education and public assistance; **43** living wage; **43B** cooperative societies (97th Amendment); **44** uniform civil code; **47** nutrition and public health, prohibition of intoxicants; **48A** environment, forests and wildlife (42nd); **50** separation of judiciary from executive.

**Eleven Fundamental Duties**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** on the **Swaran Singh Committee's** recommendation, with 51A(k) added by the 86th. Non-justiciable, but the **Verma Committee (1999)** listed existing statutes that operationalise them, and courts use them as an interpretive aid.

**53** executive power vested in the President; **74** Council of Ministers **aid and advise**, binding after the **42nd Amendment**, with a **one-time return for reconsideration** added by the 44th; **75(3)** collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; **76** Attorney General; **78** the PM's duty to communicate Council decisions to the President — the constitutional basis of the President's right to be informed.

**Pardoning power** — President (72) covers court martial, offences against Union law, and **all death sentences**; Governor (161) is narrower. It is an **executive act, exercised on ministerial advice**, and is **judicially reviewable on limited grounds** — non-application of mind, mala fides, or irrelevant considerations. Undue delay in deciding a mercy petition is a ground to commute.
items.s: Maru Ram (1980) / Epuru Sudhakar (2006) / Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)

items.d: **Ordinance-making power** of the President and Governor, exercisable only when the legislature is not in session and immediate action is necessary. *Krishna Kumar Singh* (2017) held that **re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution** and that ordinances must be laid before the legislature — satisfaction is subject to judicial review. Bihar's 256 re-promulgated ordinances over 1967-81 is the standing example.

**155** appointed by the President; **156** holds office **during the President's pleasure** — no fixed tenure; **163** aids-and-advises except where he acts in his discretion, and **the question of what falls in discretion is non-justiciable in form but reviewable in substance**; **164(1)** appoints the CM; **200** assent to bills; **361** immunity. The Sarkaria, Punchhi and Venkatachaliah reports all recommended appointment from a panel proposed by the state and removal only for proven misconduct.

The Governor may assent, withhold assent, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or **reserve it for the President**. The **first proviso requires a return 'as soon as possible'**; if the House passes it again, the Governor **shall not withhold assent**. The Supreme Court has read **timelines into what the text leaves open** and held that indefinite inaction — the 'pocket veto' — is unconstitutional. The Presidential Reference of 2025 arose from this line of cases.
items.s: State of Punjab v. Governor (2023) / State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (2025)

items.d: President's Rule on failure of constitutional machinery. *S.R. Bommai* (1994) made the proclamation **justiciable**, held that the **floor of the House is the only test of majority**, that the Assembly may be dissolved only **after both Houses of Parliament approve**, and that **secularism is a basic feature** — a state government acting against secularism can be dismissed. Recommended for use only in extreme cases by the **Sarkaria Commission**.

**79** Parliament = President + two Houses; **80** Rajya Sabha up to 250 (238 elected by **single transferable vote** by state assemblies + 12 nominated); **81** Lok Sabha up to 550; **83** terms — LS five years, RS a permanent body with **one-third retiring every two years**; **88** ministers and the AG have the right to speak in either House.

**100** quorum is **one-tenth** of the total membership; **108** **joint sitting** to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary or financial (not money) bill — used only **three times**: Dowry Prohibition Act (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978) and the **POTA (2002)**. The Speaker presides over a joint sitting.

**109** money bills originate only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha has **14 days and only recommendatory power**; **110** defines a money bill and the **Speaker's certification is final**; **112** Annual Financial Statement; **113-114** demands for grants and the Appropriation Bill; **266** Consolidated Fund; **267** Contingency Fund; **117** prior recommendation of the President for financial bills. The money-bill route used for Aadhaar was upheld in *Puttaswamy (Aadhaar)* but doubted in *Rojer Mathew* and referred to a larger bench.

Freedom of speech in Parliament and immunity from proceedings for anything said or any vote given. **Sita Soren (2024)**, a **seven-judge bench, overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**, holding that a legislator who takes a **bribe for a vote or speech enjoys no immunity** — the offence is complete on acceptance and is not 'essential to' the legislative function. Privileges remain **uncodified**, the standing reform demand.
items.s: Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)

items.d: Inserted by the **52nd Amendment, 1985**; the **91st Amendment, 2003** deleted the split (one-third) exception and required a **merger of two-thirds**. *Kihoto Hollohan* (1992) upheld it but made the **Speaker's decision subject to judicial review**; *Keisham Meghachandra* (2020) said the Speaker should decide **within three months** and suggested an independent tribunal; *Subhash Desai* (2023) held that a **Whip is appointed by the party, not the legislature party**.

**PAC (1921, 22 members, chaired by the Opposition by convention)**, **Estimates Committee (1950, 30 members, LS only — 'continuous economy committee')**, **COPU (1964, 22)**; **24 Department-Related Standing Committees since 1993** (16 LS + 8 RS, 31 members each), which examine demands for grants, bills and long-term policy. Ministers are not members of DRSCs. Committee scrutiny of bills has fallen sharply — the standing critique of parliamentary decline.
items.s: Rules of Procedure / PRS Legislative Research

items.d: **124** establishment and appointment; **124A-C** were the NJAC provisions struck down in 2015; **126** acting CJI; **127-128** ad hoc and retired judges; **129** court of record with contempt power; **131** original jurisdiction in Centre-state disputes; **136** **Special Leave Petition**, the discretionary residual power; **137** review; **141** law declared is binding on all courts; **142** **complete justice**; **143** advisory jurisdiction, which the Court may decline.

Power to pass any decree necessary for **complete justice**. Used for the **Ayodhya** settlement, the **Babri** structure, the **2G** cancellation, dissolving marriages on **irretrievable breakdown** (*Shilpa Sailesh*, 2023), and in *State of Punjab v. Governor* to fix timelines. Also the subject of the sharpest separation-of-powers criticism — powers under 142 cannot **supplant substantive law**.

High Courts; **Art. 226 is wider than Art. 32** — it issues writs for fundamental rights **and for 'any other purpose'**, and its territorial reach extends to where the cause of action arises. *L. Chandra Kumar* (1997) held that the **High Courts' power of judicial review under 226/227 is part of the basic structure** and tribunals cannot oust it.

**246** and the **Seventh Schedule**: Union List 97, State List 59 (originally 66), Concurrent List 52 (originally 47). **248** residuary power with the Union; **249** RS resolution by two-thirds enabling Parliament to legislate on a State List item in the national interest; **250** during emergency; **252** two or more states requesting; **253** to implement international agreements; **254** **repugnancy**, with state law prevailing if it receives **Presidential assent**. Doctrines: **pith and substance, colourable legislation, harmonious construction**.

**262** inter-state **river water disputes** — Parliament may bar the jurisdiction of all courts, done by the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; **263** empowers the President to establish an **Inter-State Council** — done in 1990 on the **Sarkaria Commission's** recommendation. The ISC is an advisory, recommendatory body that has met rarely; the **Punchhi Commission** wanted it strengthened into the primary forum for federal consultation.

Created by the **101st Amendment, 2016**. Voting: **Centre one-third, all states together two-thirds, decisions by a three-fourths majority**; quorum one-half. *Mohit Minerals* (2022) held that **the Council's recommendations are persuasive, not binding**, because both Parliament and state legislatures have simultaneous power under Art. 246A — described by the Court as **'cooperative federalism as dialogue'**.
items.s: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022)

items.d: **280** Finance Commission every five years — devolution, grants-in-aid under Art. 275, and measures to augment state funds for local bodies. **148-151** the **CAG** — appointed by the President, removable like a SC judge, salary charged on the Consolidated Fund, **barred from further office** under the Union or a state after retirement; reports go to the President/Governor and are examined by the PAC.

UPSC and State PSCs; **316** appointment by the President/Governor, **at least half the members must have held office under the Government for ten years**; **317** removal **only by the President on a Supreme Court reference**; **319** post-retirement bar (a UPSC chairman is ineligible for any further government employment); **320** functions; **322** expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund; **323** annual report laid before the legislature with a memorandum on non-acceptance of advice.

**Tribunals** (42nd Amendment) — administrative tribunals (323A, Parliament only) and other-matter tribunals (323B). **324** vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the **Election Commission**; the CEC and ECs are now appointed under the **CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023**, enacted after *Anoop Baranwal* (2023) had prescribed a CJI-inclusive panel. The CEC can be removed only like a SC judge; other ECs only on the CEC's recommendation.

**NCSC (338)**, **NCST (338A, created by the 89th Amendment, 2003)** and **NCBC (338B, given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment, 2018)** — all have the powers of a civil court and must be consulted on major policy affecting their groups. **350B** Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. The **105th Amendment, 2021** restored the states' power to identify their own SEBCs after *Maratha Reservation* (2021).

**73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992** — three tiers above 20 lakh population, five-year terms, **State Election Commission (243K/243ZA)**, **State Finance Commission every five years (243I/243Y)**, **one-third seats for women** (many states now 50%), **Eleventh Schedule 29 subjects** and **Twelfth Schedule 18 subjects**, **District Planning Committee (243ZD)** and **Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE)**. Devolution of functions, funds and functionaries remains discretionary — the core weakness.

**Fifth Schedule** — Scheduled Areas in ten states, Governor's report to the President, **Tribes Advisory Council**, and the Governor's power to modify central or state laws for the area. **Sixth Schedule** — **Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram** with legislative, judicial and financial powers over land, forests and customary law. **PESA, 1996** extends Part IX to Scheduled Areas with the gram sabha as the competent authority.

sections.h: The Case-Law Bank — Holding in One Line

items.d: Held a constitutional amendment is **'law' under Article 13? No** — 'law' in Art. 13 means ordinary law, so **Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights**. Upheld the First Amendment and the Ninth Schedule.
Reaffirmed *Shankari Prasad*, but **Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar dissented** — Mudholkar first used the phrase **'basic features'**, the seed of the doctrine.

By 6:5, **reversed** the earlier position: Fundamental Rights are **transcendental and immutable**, Parliament cannot abridge them. Applied the **doctrine of prospective overruling** for the first time in India. Provoked the 24th Amendment.

**13-judge bench, 7:6.** Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution **but cannot destroy its basic structure**. Elements named across the judgments: **supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, sovereignty and unity and integrity, welfare state (Parts III-IV balance), judicial review, free and fair elections, rule of law, and the dignity of the individual**. Overruled *Golaknath*; upheld 24th, partly struck down 25th.
items.s: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)

items.t: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
items.d: Struck down **Clause 4 of the 39th Amendment**, which had put the election of the PM and Speaker beyond judicial scrutiny — **free and fair elections and judicial review are basic features**. First application of basic structure to strike down an amendment.

Struck down 42nd Amendment clauses: **limited amending power is itself a basic feature**, and the **balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles** is basic structure. Bhagwati/Chandrachud: 'the Constitution is a precious heritage; therefore you cannot destroy its identity.' Source of the **'golden triangle' of Articles 14, 19 and 21**.
Fixed **24 April 1973 — the date of *Kesavananda* — as the cut-off**: laws placed in the **Ninth Schedule before** that date are immune; those added **after** are open to basic-structure review.

Nine-judge bench confirming *Waman Rao*: any law inserted into the **Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 is testable against the basic structure**, applying the **'rights test' and the 'essence of rights' test**. Ninth Schedule is not a constitutional blank cheque.

Nine judges. **Article 356 proclamation is justiciable**; majority is tested **only on the floor of the House**; the Assembly may be dissolved **only after both Houses approve**; the Court can restore a dismissed government; and **secularism is a basic feature**.

Struck down the **99th Amendment and the NJAC Act** 4:1 — **primacy of the judiciary in judicial appointments is part of the independence of the judiciary and hence basic structure**. Restored the collegium; the promised Memorandum of Procedure remains unfinalised, which is the live reform question.

groups.g: Judicial review, PIL and the judicial process

items.d: Read the Fundamental Rights as **watertight compartments** and upheld preventive detention — 'procedure established by law' meant any enacted procedure. **Overruled in substance by *Maneka Gandhi*.** Fazl Ali J.'s lone dissent later became the law.

Passport impounding case. Articles **14, 19 and 21 are interlinked** and any procedure under Art. 21 must be **'right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive'** — imported **substantive due process** and made *audi alteram partem* implicit in Art. 21. The most cited case in Indian constitutional law.

The **Habeas Corpus case** — held during the Emergency that the right to move a court under Art. 21 stands suspended, so even an illegal detention could not be challenged. **Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent** cost him the Chief Justiceship. **Expressly overruled in *Puttaswamy* (2017)** and called 'seriously flawed'. The 44th Amendment made Art. 20 and 21 non-suspendable.

**First Judges case** — diluted 'consultation' with the CJI to mere consultation, and, more importantly, **relaxed *locus standi* to found Public Interest Litigation**: any public-spirited person may move the court on behalf of those unable to. Bhagwati J.'s judgment is the charter of PIL.

**1993** created the **collegium**, reading 'consultation' as **'concurrence'** and giving the judiciary primacy; **1998**, on a Presidential reference under Art. 143, expanded the collegium to the **CJI plus four senior-most judges** and made the process one of **plurality of opinion recorded in writing**.

Judicial review under **Articles 32 and 226/227 is part of the basic structure**; tribunals may act as courts of first instance but **cannot exclude the High Court's writ jurisdiction** — appeals lie to a **Division Bench of the High Court**, not directly to the Supreme Court. Struck down the exclusion clauses of Arts. 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d).

items.t: Madras Bar Association (2014, 2020, 2021) and Rojer Mathew (2019)
items.d: The tribunal line: the **National Tax Tribunal** was struck down as an encroachment on High Court jurisdiction (2014); tribunal rules were struck down for excessive executive control over **appointment, tenure and service conditions** (*Rojer Mathew*, 2019); and the Court has repeatedly directed a **National Tribunals Commission**. Also flagged the **money-bill route** for tribunal provisions as doubtful.

**Jain hawala case** — issued 'continuing mandamus'; gave the CBI Director a **minimum two-year tenure**, created the **Central Vigilance Commission's supervisory role** over the CBI (later statutory under the CVC Act, 2003), and struck at the 'Single Directive'. The foundational judgment on investigative-agency autonomy.

Created the **curative petition** — a final remedy after dismissal of a review, to be certified by a senior counsel and heard by the three senior-most judges plus the judges who passed the order. Basis of the *Bhopal* and *Ayodhya* curative attempts.

**Access to justice is a fundamental right under Articles 14 and 21**, with four facets: the state must provide an **adjudicatory mechanism**, it must be **accessible in location**, the process must be **speedy**, and it must be **affordable**.

The first PIL on undertrials in Bihar — **speedy trial is part of Article 21**, and free legal aid is a state obligation. Led to the release of thousands of undertrials and to the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

Executive power **need not rest on a prior statute** — it extends to all matters on which the legislature can legislate, provided it does not violate the Constitution or infringe rights. Also stated that India does not follow a rigid separation of powers.

Seven judges: the **President and Governor are constitutional heads** who exercise powers **only on the aid and advice** of the Council of Ministers, except in the few situations of constitutional discretion. Settled Indian parliamentary convention.

Arunachal Pradesh: the **Governor cannot summon, prorogue or dissolve the House at his own discretion** or advance an Assembly session against ministerial advice; **Article 163 does not give a general discretionary power**. Restored the dismissed government — the first such restoration since *Bommai*.

Maharashtra: the **Governor was wrong to call a floor test** on the material available, since a party's internal dissent is not a loss of confidence; a **Whip is appointed by the political party, not the legislature party**; but the Court could **not restore the government** because the CM had resigned without facing the test.

items.t: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor (2023)
items.d: The Governor **cannot sit indefinitely on bills** — the first proviso to Art. 200 requires a return 'as soon as possible', and inaction is 'not a constitutionally permissible course'. Governors are **unelected heads and cannot thwart the elected legislature**.

items.t: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (2025)
items.d: Held the Governor's reservation of ten re-passed bills illegal, deemed them assented, and read **timelines** into Articles 200-201. The Union then made a **Presidential Reference under Article 143** on whether courts may prescribe such timelines — the live federal controversy on the paper.

items.t: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018, 2023)
items.d: 2018: the LG is **bound by the aid and advice** of the Delhi government except on police, public order and land, and has **no independent decision-making power**; 'anarchy must give way to collaborative federalism'. 2023: the **elected government controls services** in Delhi — reversed within days by an **Ordinance and the GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023**, now under challenge.

**GST Council recommendations are recommendatory, not binding** — Parliament and state legislatures have **simultaneous power under Art. 246A**, and Indian federalism involves **'dialogue between cooperative and uncooperative federalism'**. Also struck down IGST on ocean freight as double taxation.

items.t: State of West Bengal v. Union of India (2024)
items.d: Held the state's suit under **Article 131** against the CBI's investigation without general consent to be **maintainable** — a major federal ruling on the DSPE Act, 1946 and the withdrawal of general consent by several states.

Nine-judge bench, 8:1: **royalty is not a tax**, and **states have the power to levy taxes on mineral rights** — one of the largest fiscal-federalism wins for states, applied with limited retrospectivity from 1 April 2005.

Upheld the abrogation: **Article 370 was a temporary provision**, Jammu & Kashmir **retained no element of internal sovereignty** after accession, and the President's power under 370(3) survived the dissolution of the Constituent Assembly. Directed **restoration of statehood** and **elections** — held in 2024.

Upheld the **Tenth Schedule** but struck down Paragraph 7 (the ouster of judicial review) for want of ratification; the **Speaker acts as a tribunal** and the decision is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, perversity or violation of natural justice, though **not at an interlocutory stage**.

Speakers should decide disqualification petitions **within three months** save in exceptional circumstances, and Parliament should **consider an independent tribunal headed by a retired judge** because a Speaker belongs to a party.

'Cash for query' expulsions — Parliament **has the power to expel members**, but the exercise of privilege is **subject to judicial review** for illegality or unconstitutionality. Privilege is not absolute.

The classic advisory opinion on the conflict between the **UP Assembly's privileges and the High Court's jurisdiction** — held that the House cannot be the sole judge of its privileges when fundamental rights and the courts' powers are engaged.

1998 had granted **immunity to a legislator who took a bribe and then voted**, an outcome widely criticised as immunising corruption. **Sita Soren (2024), seven judges, unanimously overruled it** — bribery is not protected by Arts. 105/194 because it is **not essential to casting a vote or making a speech**, and the offence is complete on acceptance.

The **Election Commission's plenary power under Article 324** fills gaps in the law, but must be exercised **consistently with natural justice and the rule of law**; also the principle that an order must be judged by the reasons recorded in it, not by later affidavits.

Constitution Bench directed appointment of the **CEC and ECs by a committee of the PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI** until Parliament legislated. Parliament responded with the **CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023**, replacing the CJI with a **Union Cabinet Minister** — the live controversy on ECI independence.

items.t: Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and PUCL (2003)
items.d: Candidates must disclose **assets, liabilities, education and criminal antecedents** — the voter's **right to know is part of Article 19(1)(a)**; the attempt to nullify it through Section 33B of the RPA was struck down. **PUCL (2013)** added **NOTA**.

Struck down **Section 8(4) of the RPA, 1951**: a convicted legislator is **disqualified immediately on conviction**, with no three-month protection to file an appeal. Paired with *Public Interest Foundation* (2018), which requires publication of criminal antecedents by candidates and parties.

items.t: Electoral Bonds — ADR v. Union of India (2024)
items.d: Struck down the **Electoral Bond Scheme** unanimously: anonymous corporate funding violates the **voter's right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**, and the removal of the **7.5% profit cap** on company donations was **manifestly arbitrary**. Directed the SBI to disclose all bond data to the ECI. The leading recent judgment on political finance.

By 4:3, read **Section 123(3) of the RPA** purposively: an appeal for votes on grounds of **religion, race, caste, community or language — of the candidate *or the voter* — is a corrupt practice**. Elections are a 'secular exercise'.

Upheld the removal of the **domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha members** and the shift to **open ballot** — held that the RS is not a federal chamber in a rigid sense and that an open ballot curbs cross-voting without violating free and fair elections.

Communal caste-based reservation in college admissions was struck down as violating Art. 29(2) — provoking the **First Amendment, 1951**, which added **Article 15(4)**. The first Constitutional amendment traceable to a judgment.

**Mandal case, nine judges.** Upheld 27% OBC reservation; **caste can be a starting point for identifying a class**; excluded the **creamy layer**; capped total reservation at **50% save in extraordinary circumstances**; barred reservation in **promotions** (later reversed by the 77th Amendment) and held that reservation cannot apply to **super-speciality posts**. The single most important social-justice judgment.

Upheld reservation in promotion but subjected it to three conditions — the state must show **backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and no impairment of administrative efficiency**, with quantifiable data.

**Removed the requirement to prove the backwardness of SC/STs** (following *Indra Sawhney*'s logic that SC/STs are presumed backward), but **applied the creamy-layer principle to SC/STs for promotions**. 2022 clarified that the unit for collecting data is the **cadre**.

Upheld the **103rd Amendment's 10% EWS quota** 3:2 — reservation solely on **economic criteria is permissible**, the **50% ceiling is not inviolable**, and excluding SC/ST/OBC from EWS does not violate the basic structure. The dissents (Bhat and Lalit JJ.) called the exclusion 'exclusionary and discriminatory'.

items.t: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)
items.d: Seven judges, 6:1, **overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2005)**: **sub-classification within Scheduled Castes is permissible** because SCs are not a homogenous class, provided it rests on **quantifiable data and not political expediency**; several judges also urged applying the **creamy layer** to SCs/STs.

Struck down Maharashtra's SEBC quota for **breaching the 50% ceiling without extraordinary circumstances**, and held that after the **102nd Amendment only the President could notify SEBCs** — reversed by the **105th Amendment, 2021**, restoring state power.

*Vishaka* laid down binding guidelines against **sexual harassment at the workplace**, drawing on **CEDAW** — judicial legislation to fill a statutory vacuum; codified as the **POSH Act, 2013**. *Aureliano Fernandes* (2023) noted the 'sorry state of affairs' in the constitution of Internal Complaints Committees and directed compliance audits.

A **daughter is a coparcener by birth** under the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act — the right is **unobstructed heritage**, so it applies **whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005**. Settled the conflict between *Prakash v. Phulavati* and *Danamma*.

**Accessibility is a component of Article 21** — directed that the **mandatory accessibility standards** under the RPwD Act, 2016 be framed and enforced, distinguishing **non-negotiable rules from aspirational guidelines**. The leading disability-rights judgment after the shift to the social model of disability.

Recognised **transgender persons as a third gender**, upheld the **right to self-identification of gender** as part of Arts. 14, 15, 19 and 21, and directed OBC-style reservation in education and employment. Statutory follow-up: **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019**.

Nine judges, unanimous: **privacy is a fundamental right intrinsic to Article 21 and the whole of Part III**, with informational, bodily and decisional autonomy dimensions. Any restriction must pass the **four-fold proportionality test — legality, legitimate aim, necessity/rational connection, and least restrictive means with procedural safeguards**. Overruled *M.P. Sharma* and *Kharak Singh*; expressly overruled *ADM Jabalpur*.

Upheld Aadhaar for **subsidies, benefits and services funded from the Consolidated Fund and for PAN/income tax**, but struck down **Section 57** (private-party use) and the mandatory bank/mobile linkage; upheld its passage as a **money bill** 4:1 — the point Chandrachud J. called 'a fraud on the Constitution' in dissent.

Struck down **Section 66A of the IT Act** as vague and overbroad — distinguished **advocacy from incitement**, held that only incitement can be restricted under Art. 19(2); read down **Section 79** and the intermediary rules to require a **court or government order** for takedown. The foundational online-speech judgment.

Kashmir internet shutdown: **freedom of speech and of trade over the internet is protected under Arts. 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g)**; **indefinite suspension is impermissible**; every order must be **published, reasoned and subject to periodic review** by a committee. India remains the country with the most internet shutdowns globally.

Upheld **sedition (IPC 124A) but read it down** — only speech with a **tendency to incite violence or public disorder** is criminal, not mere criticism of government. The section was kept in abeyance in 2022 (*S.G. Vombatkere*) and reappears as **Section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** ('acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity').

By 4:1: **no additional restrictions on free speech beyond Art. 19(2)** can be imposed on ministers; a statement by a minister is **not vicariously attributable to the government**; and **fundamental rights under Arts. 19 and 21 are enforceable even against private persons** — a significant horizontal-application ruling.

Decriminalised consensual same-sex relations by reading down **Section 377** — 'constitutional morality must prevail over social morality'; identity, autonomy and dignity are protected. Chandrachud J.: the Constitution protects the **'right to love'**. Later, *Supriyo* (2023) declined to recognise same-sex **marriage** as a matter for the legislature.
Struck down **adultery (IPC 497)** — it treated the wife as the husband's property, denied women agency and was **manifestly arbitrary**; 'a husband is not the master of his wife'.

Recognised the **right to die with dignity** as part of Art. 21 — **passive euthanasia and advance medical directives ('living wills')** are permissible, with safeguards simplified in the 2023 clarification.

*D.K. Basu* laid down **eleven binding requirements for arrest and detention** (memo of arrest, informing a relative, medical examination, right to counsel) — now largely in the CrPC/BNSS. *Nilabati Behera* established **compensation in public law for custodial death** as a remedy under Arts. 32/226, distinct from a civil suit, and rejected sovereign immunity.

On **preventive detention**: it is 'a draconian measure and an exception to Articles 19 and 21'; the courts must satisfy themselves of the **live and proximate link** between the grounds and the order, and **ordinary criminal law must be shown to be inadequate**. The best recent citation for a preventive-detention answer.

Great Indian Bustard case: recognised the **right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change** as part of **Articles 14 and 21**, drawing on Arts. 48A and 51A(g) — the first explicit constitutional climate right in India. Also balanced species conservation against India's renewable-energy commitments.

Origin of the **'essential religious practices' doctrine** — the state may regulate secular activities associated with religion but not what is **essential to the religion itself**, and what is essential is decided by reference to the doctrines of that religion. Criticised for making judges arbiters of theology.

**Secularism is a basic feature**; the state has no religion, and religion cannot be mixed with **secular activities of the state**. Indian secularism is 'principled distance' — equal respect rather than the Western wall of separation.

4:1: the exclusion of women aged 10-50 was **not an essential religious practice** and violated Arts. 14, 15, 17, 21 and 25; **constitutional morality prevails over social morality**. Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent — that courts should not test the rationality of faith — is essential for balance. Referred to a nine-judge bench on larger questions in 2020.

A divorced Muslim woman is entitled to maintenance under **Section 125 CrPC**, a secular provision. Reversed by the **Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986**, but *Danial Latifi* (2001) read the Act to require a **reasonable and fair provision for life**. *Shabana Bano* and later rulings confirm access to Section 125 (now **Section 144 BNSS**).

Both judgments **urged a Uniform Civil Code** under Art. 44 — *Sarla Mudgal* held that conversion to Islam does not dissolve a Hindu marriage and a second marriage is bigamy; *John Vallamattom* struck down Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act as discriminating against Christians.

By 3:2, struck down **instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat)** — held **manifestly arbitrary** under Art. 14 by the majority; codified as the **Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019**, which made the practice a criminal offence.

Seven judges, 4:3, **overruled *Azeez Basha* (1968)**: an institution does not lose minority status merely because it was **created by statute**; the test is who **founded** it and for whose benefit — the **indicia test** of establishment and administration. The question of AMU's own status was left to a regular bench.

Eleven judges: minority status is determined **state-wise**; unaided private institutions have **autonomy in admissions and fees** subject to the prohibition of profiteering and capitation fees; the state cannot impose quotas on unaided private institutions — which prompted the **93rd Amendment (Art. 15(5))**.

The **Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991** freezes the religious character of places of worship as on **15 August 1947** (excepting Ayodhya). *Ayodhya* (2019) called the Act a legislative instrument that **protects secularism as a basic feature**; its validity and the maintainability of suits under it are pending.

On the RTI Act's own institutions — directed **transparent appointment of Information Commissioners**, publication of vacancies and criteria, and timely filling of posts; noted that vacancies were themselves defeating the Act. High vacancy in Information Commissions remains the standing critique.

items.t: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande (2012) and CPIO v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019)
items.d: *Deshpande* held that service records and personal details are **exempt under Section 8(1)(j)** unless a larger public interest is shown — the most-cited exemption ruling. *Subhash Chandra Agarwal* held that the **CJI's office is a public authority under the RTI Act**, with judicial independence to be balanced against transparency.

Seven binding directives on **police reform**: State Security Commission, **minimum two-year tenure for the DGP and field officers**, **separation of investigation from law and order**, a **Police Establishment Board** for transfers, a **Police Complaints Authority**, and a National Security Commission. Compliance by states remains partial — the model example of judicial direction without executive follow-through.

Directed a **Civil Services Board** to advise on transfers and postings, a **minimum fixed tenure** for civil servants, and that **oral instructions be recorded in writing** — the judicial answer to political interference in administration.

Introduced the **arbitrariness doctrine**: 'equality is a dynamic concept... it cannot be cribbed, cabined and confined within traditional and doctrinaire limits'; **equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies**. Arose from a Chief Secretary's transfer — a service matter that changed Article 14 jurisprudence.

items.t: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985)
items.d: On the second proviso to **Article 311(2)**: the three exceptions (conviction on a criminal charge, impracticability of holding an inquiry, and security of the state) dispense with the inquiry, but the decision must be based on **recorded reasons** and is subject to judicial review.

Upheld the **FCRA (Amendment) Act, 2020** — including the bar on **sub-granting** and the mandatory SBI New Delhi account — holding that **no one has a fundamental right to receive foreign contribution** and that foreign funding can affect the political and public interest. The key case on the NGO regulation question.

items.t: Common Cause v. Union of India (2018, CBI Director)
items.d: The line of cases on the **CBI Director's appointment and tenure** — appointment by a committee of the **PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI** under the DSPE Act, and the controversy over the divestiture of powers, which the Court held could not be done without the committee's concurrence.

Information within **30 days** (48 hours if life or liberty is involved); **Section 4** proactive disclosure; **Section 8** exemptions with a **public-interest override**; **Section 24** exempts intelligence and security organisations except for corruption and human-rights allegations. The **RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019** let the Centre fix the **tenure, salary and service conditions of Information Commissioners** — the central criticism. The **DPDP Act, 2023** amended Section 8(1)(j) to exempt all personal information, further narrowing the Act.

A **chairperson plus up to 8 members, half judicial and half from SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women**; jurisdiction covers the **PM with exclusions** (international relations, security, public order, atomic energy, space) and requires a **two-thirds bench approval**; power of **attachment and confiscation** of assets; mandates **states to set up Lokayuktas within a year**. Criticism: delayed appointment (first Lokpal only in 2019), weak prosecution wing, and the dilution of the whistle-blower link.

Passed but **never brought into force** — no rules notified, and the **2015 amendment bill** would bar disclosures touching ten exempt categories including sovereignty and commercial confidence. The gap is the standing example of 'legislation without implementation'.

The **2018 amendment** made **bribe-giving an offence**, covered **commercial organisations**, required **prior approval under Section 17A** before any enquiry into a public servant's official decisions, and extended the **Section 19** sanction requirement to retired officials. Criticised for protecting decision-makers; defended as the fix for 'decision paralysis'.

Made the CVC statutory (it existed from 1964 on the **Santhanam Committee's** recommendation). Multi-member body appointed by the President on the advice of the **PM, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition**; **supervises the CBI's investigation** of PC Act offences; the CVO in each ministry reports to it.

**Digital Personal Data Protection Act** — consent-based processing with **legitimate uses** exemptions, **Data Fiduciary** duties, **Consent Managers**, rights to access, correction, erasure and grievance redress, penalties up to **₹250 crore**, and a **Data Protection Board of India**. Criticised for **broad state exemptions under Section 17** and the dilution of RTI Section 8(1)(j). Rules notified in 2025.

Institutionalises **pre-litigation mediation** (voluntary after the 2023 revision), the **Mediation Council of India**, a **180-day** timeline, and enforceability of the settlement agreement as a court decree. Complements **Section 89 CPC**, the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** (Lok Adalats) and the **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008**.

**Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (replacing IPC), **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita** (CrPC) and **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam** (Evidence Act), in force from **1 July 2024**. Key changes: **community service** as a punishment, **Zero FIR and e-FIR**, **timelines for charge-sheet, judgment (45 days) and framing of charges**, **forensic visits mandatory for offences carrying 7+ years**, sedition replaced by **Section 152**, and organised crime and terrorism defined in the general penal code for the first time.

Legal entitlement to subsidised grain for **75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population** — about **80 crore people**; **5 kg per person per month** for priority households and **35 kg per household** for Antyodaya; **maternity benefit of ₹6,000**; grain provided **free under PMGKAY** since 2023, extended to 2028. Also mandates **grievance redress officers and vigilance committees**. Coverage still rests on **Census 2011** population — the standing exclusion critique.

**100 days of guaranteed wage employment** per rural household, work within **5 km**, wages within **15 days** else compensation, **unemployment allowance** if work is not provided in 15 days, **one-third participation by women** (actual participation is over 50%), and **social audit by the gram sabha** as a statutory requirement. Demand-driven and rights-based — the world's largest such programme. Being restructured as the **VB-G RAM G Act, 2025**.

Free and compulsory education for **6-14**; **25% reservation in private unaided schools** for disadvantaged groups with state reimbursement; **no detention till Class 8** (relaxed by the **2019 amendment**, which allows detention in Classes 5 and 8 after a re-examination); prohibits **screening, capitation fees, physical punishment and teacher deployment for non-educational work** other than census, elections and disaster relief; **PTR and infrastructure norms** in the Schedule.

Recognises **individual forest rights**, **community forest rights** and, crucially, **Community Forest Resource rights (Section 3(1)(i))** with the gram sabha as the authority to protect and manage; also recognises rights of **Other Traditional Forest Dwellers** with a 75-year residence test. Basis of the **Niyamgiri** gram sabha veto. Low CFR recognition is the implementation gap.

Expanded disabilities from 7 to **21**, adopted the **social model** in line with the **UNCRPD**, provided **4% reservation in government jobs and 5% in higher education**, **accessibility standards**, and the concept of **reasonable accommodation**; recognises **high-support needs** and creates State/Chief Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities. *Rajive Raturi* (2024) enforced its accessibility rules.

**Decriminalised attempted suicide** (presumption of severe stress), gave every person a **right to access mental healthcare**, introduced **advance directives** and a **nominated representative**, and set up **Mental Health Review Boards**. Aligned with the UNCRPD. India's treatment gap for mental illness remains around 70-90%.

items.t: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007
items.d: Obliges children and heirs to maintain parents and senior citizens; **maintenance tribunals** decide within 90 days; a **transfer of property can be voided** if the transferee neglects the elder; also provides for old-age homes in every district. The 2019 amendment bill sought to remove the maintenance ceiling and widen 'children' to include stepchildren and in-laws.

Statutory recognition of vending as a livelihood under **Art. 19(1)(g)**; **Town Vending Committees with 40% vendor representation**, a survey of all vendors, vending certificates, and a **prohibition on eviction without survey and rehabilitation**. Complemented by **PM SVANidhi** micro-credit.

Right to **self-perceived gender identity** with a certificate from the District Magistrate, prohibition of discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, and a **National Council for Transgender Persons**. Criticised for the certification requirement and for lighter punishment for offences against transgender persons than under general law.

**Selection Committee: the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM, and the Leader of the Opposition** — replacing the CJI whom *Anoop Baranwal* had included; a **Search Committee** headed by the Cabinet Secretary shortlists five names; **status and salary equal to a Supreme Court judge**; **removal of the CEC only like a Supreme Court judge**.

The CBI's only legal basis — it is **not a statutory body created by its own Act**. **Section 6** requires the **state's consent** for the CBI to investigate within its territory; several states have **withdrawn general consent**. Calcutta HC and the SC (*West Bengal v. Union of India*, 2024) have engaged the resulting federal question. **Section 4A** governs the Director's appointment; **Section 4B** the two-year minimum tenure.

Creates the **NHRC** — chaired by a **former CJI or a Supreme Court judge** (widened by the 2019 amendment), with the **chairpersons of NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCPCR, NCBC and the CIC and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities as deemed members**; **term 3 years or up to age 70**. Powers are **recommendatory**, it cannot inquire into a matter **more than one year old**, and it can only **seek a report from the armed forces**. That trio of limits is the standard critique.

Enacted under **Article 323A** — the **Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)** with 17 benches, and state tribunals on request. After *L. Chandra Kumar* (1997), an appeal lies to the **Division Bench of the High Court**, so the object of reducing the burden on High Courts was substantially defeated.

Abolished nine appellate tribunals (including FTAT, AAIFR and the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal), fixed a **four-year term and a minimum age of 50** for members, and re-enacted provisions the Supreme Court had struck down in *Madras Bar Association (2020)* — the sharpest recent instance of a legislative override of a judgment.

Regulates foreign contributions to associations. The **2020 amendment** barred **sub-granting to other FCRA entities**, cut permissible administrative expenses from 50% to **20%**, made **Aadhaar of office-bearers mandatory**, and required an **exclusive FCRA account at SBI, New Delhi Main Branch**. Upheld in *Noel Harper* (2022). Registrations of thousands of NGOs have lapsed or been cancelled since.

Applies where the scheduled offence involves **₹100 crore or more** and the person has left India to avoid prosecution; permits **confiscation of all assets, including benami and foreign property, without conviction**, and bars the fugitive from filing or defending civil claims. Used against Vijay Mallya, Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi.

Enacted under **Article 262**; the **2019 amendment bill** proposed a **single standing tribunal with multiple benches**, a **Disputes Resolution Committee** for negotiated settlement first, and strict timelines (one year, extendable by six months) — a response to tribunals such as Cauvery taking decades. The Act **bars the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court** under Art. 262(2), though SLPs still reach it.

items.t: Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023
items.d: Enacted after the Supreme Court's services judgment; creates the **National Capital Civil Services Authority** (CM plus the Chief Secretary and Principal Home Secretary, deciding by majority) with the **LG's discretion final** — effectively reversing the ruling. Pending before a Constitution Bench; the leading example of the legislature-versus-judiciary federalism conflict.

groups.g: International instruments India is party to

items.d: India is a party to the **ICCPR and ICESCR (both ratified 1979)**; the **UDHR (1948)** is declaratory and the source of Article 21 jurisprudence via *Maneka* and *Vishaka*. India has **not ratified** the Convention Against Torture (signed 1997), the Refugee Convention 1951, or ILO Conventions 87 and 98 on freedom of association.

India ratified **CEDAW in 1993 with declarations** on Articles 5(a) and 16(1) (non-interference in personal law) and on compulsory registration of marriage. *Vishaka* used CEDAW to fill the domestic vacuum, establishing that **international conventions consistent with fundamental rights can be read into them**.

**UNCRC ratified 1992** — basis of the JJ Act, POCSO and the child labour amendments; **UNCRPD ratified 2007** — basis of the RPwD Act, 2016 and its shift from the medical to the **social model of disability**.

**UN Convention Against Corruption**, ratified by India in **2011** — the trigger for the Lokpal Act, the amendment criminalising bribe-giving, and the Prevention of Money Laundering framework. Also the basis of mutual legal assistance in asset recovery.

India is **not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol** and has **no domestic refugee law** — refugees are governed by the Foreigners Act, 1946 (now the **Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025**), leaving status determination executive and ad hoc. Yet India has hosted Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils, Chakmas and Rohingya — the practice-versus-law gap is the answer's core point. *NHRC v. State of Arunachal Pradesh* (1996) held **Article 21 applies to non-citizens**.

247 recommendations on Centre-state relations: use **Article 356 as a last resort** and only after a warning, appoint the Governor from **outside the state and not a recent politician** and in **consultation with the Chief Minister**, make the **Inter-State Council under Article 263 a permanent body** (done in 1990), and consult states before legislating on Concurrent List subjects.
