Upheld the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code** in full — including **Section 29A** (barring defaulting promoters from bidding) and the distinction between financial and operational creditors — describing the IBC as having shifted the paradigm so that '**the defaulter's paradise is lost**'.

*Shreya Singhal* (2015) struck down **Section 66A** and read down intermediary liability under Section 79; *Anuradha Bhasin* (2020) required shutdown orders to be **published, reasoned and reviewed**; *Puttaswamy* supplies the **proportionality test** now applied to data and surveillance questions, including the challenges to the IT Rules, 2021 and the DPDP Act's exemptions.

The **umbrella legislation** enacted after Bhopal under **Article 253** to implement the Stockholm Conference decisions — gives the Centre power to make rules on standards, hazardous substances and area restrictions, and is the parent of the **EIA Notification 2006**, the Coastal Regulation Zone rules, and the plastic, e-waste, battery and solid-waste rules. **Jan Vishwas Act, 2023** decriminalised many of its offences, replacing imprisonment with monetary penalties.

Created the **CPCB and SPCBs** — the Water Act came first and gave the boards their institutional form and 'consent to establish/operate' powers; the Air Act extended them to air quality and declared air pollution control areas. **NCAP (2019)** targets a **40% reduction in PM concentration by 2025-26** in 131 non-attainment cities, on a 2017 baseline.

**Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972** — six schedules originally, rationalised to **four by the 2022 amendment** to align with **CITES**; creates the NBWL, State Boards, NTCA and the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau. **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980**, renamed the **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 2023**, which exempted land within 100 km of international borders for strategic projects and narrowed the *Godavarman* definition — read down by the Supreme Court in 2024. **Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended 2023)** — NBA, SBBs and **Biodiversity Management Committees**, and access and benefit-sharing under the **Nagoya Protocol**.

India was the **third country after Australia and New Zealand** to set up a specialised environmental court. Composition: judicial and expert members; disposal within **6 months**; applies **sustainable development, the precautionary principle and polluter pays** by statute (Section 20); can hear matters under seven listed environmental Acts — **but not the Wild Life Act, the Forest Rights Act or the Indian Forest Act**, the standing jurisdictional gap. Appeals lie to the Supreme Court.

**Energy Conservation Act, 2001**, amended in **2022** to create the **carbon credit trading scheme**, mandate a minimum share of non-fossil energy for designated consumers, and extend the Energy Conservation Building Code to residential buildings. **Electricity Act, 2003** — unbundling, open access, CERC/SERCs, and the RPO obligation. **Atomic Energy Act, 1962** and the **Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010**, whose Section 17(b) supplier-liability clause is the obstacle to foreign reactor supply.

**Essential Commodities Act, 1955** — stock limits and the 2020 amendment (since lapsed with the farm laws' repeal); **APMC Acts** are state law, with the **model APLM Act, 2017** and the **contract farming model Act, 2018** as the Centre's persuasion route; **PPVFR Act, 2001** — India's *sui generis* alternative to UPOV, uniquely recognising **farmers' rights to save, use, exchange and sell seed**; **FSSAI** under the FSS Act, 2006; and the **Seeds Bill**, pending for two decades.

**National Commission on Farmers** — five reports. Core recommendations: MSP at **C2 plus 50%**, a **National Land Use Advisory Service**, distribution of ceiling-surplus and waste land, credit at 4%, an **Agriculture Risk Fund**, and a **National Food Security Act**. The C2+50% formula is the single most-quoted unimplemented recommendation in Indian agriculture.

On restructuring the FCI: found that **only about 6% of farmers benefit from MSP procurement**, recommended deregulation of grain trade, **cash transfers instead of PDS grain in phases**, reducing NFSA coverage from 67% to **40%**, and outsourcing FCI's procurement in states that have built their own capacity.

**Doubling Farmers' Income by 2022** — fourteen volumes. Identified **seven sources of income growth** (crop productivity, livestock productivity, resource-use efficiency, cropping intensity, diversification to high-value crops, better real prices, and shift from farm to non-farm work) and established that income, not output, is the correct policy objective. Concluded that **more than half the growth must come from non-price factors**.

items.t: M.S. Swaminathan vs the Green Revolution critiques
items.d: The Green Revolution (1966-67 onwards, **Norman Borlaug's** HYV seeds via the **IARI**, C. Subramaniam as minister, Swaminathan as scientist) made India self-sufficient but produced **regional concentration in Punjab, Haryana and western UP**, **groundwater depletion**, **soil degradation and skewed NPK use**, and a **rice-wheat lock-in**. The **Second Green Revolution / Rainbow Revolution** framing is the answer's forward half.

**White** (milk, Operation Flood, Verghese Kurien), **Yellow** (oilseeds), **Blue** (fisheries), **Pink** (onions/pharma/prawn), **Golden** (horticulture and honey), **Silver** (eggs/poultry), **Grey** (fertiliser), **Round** (potato), **Black** (petroleum), **Evergreen Revolution** (Swaminathan's phrase for productivity growth without ecological harm). A high-yield recall list for one-mark value additions.

Recommended a shift from a single deficit target to a **debt-to-GDP anchor of 60% for general government (40% Centre, 20% states)**, a fiscal deficit of 2.5% by 2023, an **escape clause of 0.5%** for specified shocks, and a **Fiscal Council** to provide independent forecasts — the last remains unimplemented. Budget 2025-26's shift to a **debt-path anchor** is this recommendation arriving eight years late.

**Narasimham I (1991)** — reduce SLR/CRR, prudential norms, capital adequacy, four-tier banking structure; **Narasimham II (1998)** — mergers, NPA recovery, ARCs; **P.J. Nayak Committee (2014)** — dual regulation and government ownership are the root of PSB weakness, recommended a **Bank Investment Company** and professional boards; **Urjit Patel Committee (2014)** — moved India to **flexible inflation targeting** with the MPC and a 4% ±2% target.

Statutory under the **RBI Act (amended 2016)** — **six members: three from the RBI (Governor as chair with a casting vote) and three external**, appointed for four years; meets at least four times a year; the target is **4% CPI inflation with a ±2% band**, and a **failure** is three consecutive quarters outside the band, requiring a report to the government.

**Vijay Kelkar** chaired the Task Force on Direct and Indirect Taxes (2002) that shaped the **GST idea and the DTC**, the committee on **fiscal consolidation (2012)**, and the committee on **revisiting and revitalising the PPP model (2015)** — which recommended an **Infrastructure PPP Project Review Committee**, a rational risk-sharing matrix, and that PPP not be used as a means of **borrowing off-budget**. The **HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model)** in highways is the practical outcome.

**National Statistical Commission (Rangarajan Committee, 2000)** — recommended an autonomous NSC; created in 2005 but **still non-statutory**, which is why the resignations of 2019 over the withheld PLFS data mattered. **MoSPI**, **NSO** and the **CSO-NSSO merger (2019)**. The base-year revision of the GDP series to **2011-12**, with the new series being updated to a **2022-23 base**, is the live statistical reform.

On the **Economic Capital Framework** of the RBI — recommended a **contingent risk buffer of 5.5-6.5% of the balance sheet** and transfer of excess to the government, settling the reserves controversy. Cite it whenever the question touches RBI-government relations or central bank autonomy.

**Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (Madhav Gadgil, 2011)** — the **entire Western Ghats (1,29,037 km²) as an Ecologically Sensitive Area** in three zones, with a bottom-up Western Ghats Ecology Authority and gram sabha consent. **High Level Working Group (Kasturirangan, 2013)** — only **37% as ESA**, distinguishing cultural from natural landscape. States rejected both; the ESA notification has been re-issued repeatedly without finalisation — the standard example of **ecology-versus-livelihood-versus-federalism** deadlock, sharpened by the Wayanad landslides.

**Sendai Framework 2015-30** — four priorities (understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, enhancing preparedness and 'Build Back Better') and seven global targets. **PM's Ten-Point Agenda on DRR (2016)**, the **National Disaster Management Plan (2016, first aligned to Sendai)**, and the **Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019)**, an India-led global initiative now with 40+ members.

**CPCB** (statutory, 1974), **NGT** (2010), **NBWL** (WLPA), **NTCA**, **Wildlife Crime Control Bureau**, **National Biodiversity Authority** (Chennai), **CAMPA** (over ₹50,000 crore of accumulated afforestation funds, made statutory by the CAF Act, 2016), **CEC** (given statutory backing in 2023), and the **Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority**, replaced by the **Commission for Air Quality Management in the NCR (statutory, 2021)** with powers overriding the state boards.

**Stockholm (1972)** → UNEP; **Rio (1992)** → UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD, the 'Rio trio'; **Kyoto (1997, CDM)**; **Paris (2015, NDCs, bottom-up, 1.5-2°C)**; **Montreal Protocol (1987) with the Kigali Amendment (2016)** on HFCs — India's phase-down begins 2032; **Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm** on hazardous waste and POPs; **Ramsar (1971)**, **CITES (1973)**, **CMS (Bonn)**, **Minamata (mercury)**, **UNCLOS (1982) and the BBNJ Agreement (2023)**. **Kunming-Montreal GBF (2022)**: **30x30** — 30% of land and seas protected by 2030, and 23 targets.

Manufacturing's share of output and employment peaks at a **lower income level than it did for earlier industrialisers** — India's manufacturing stalled at ~17% of GVA while East Asia crossed 30%. Dani Rodrik's term; the core diagnosis in any 'why has India not become a manufacturing power' answer.

Indian firms are either very small (99%+ micro) or very large, with too few mid-sized firms — because scale triggers regulatory thresholds (the IR Code's 100/300-worker rule, factory registration, tax audit). The result is **dwarf firms that stay small deliberately** — the Economic Survey 2018-19 called them 'dwarfs, not infants'.

items.t: Twin balance sheet problem and its successor
items.d: Over-leveraged corporates and NPA-laden banks reinforcing each other (2014-19); resolved by the **IBC, recapitalisation and the AQR**, taking GNPA from 11.2% to ~2.5%. The Economic Survey then described a **'twin balance sheet advantage'** — clean bank and corporate books enabling a fresh investment cycle.

Public capex **crowds in** private investment when it builds enabling infrastructure (capex multiplier ~2.45 against ~0.98 for revenue spending); it **crowds out** when government borrowing raises the cost of capital. The empirical claim behind the ₹11.21 lakh crore capex push.

**Revenue deficit** (the government borrowing to consume), **effective revenue deficit** (net of grants for capital assets), **primary deficit** (fiscal deficit minus interest — the *new* borrowing), and **debt sustainability**, which holds when the **growth rate exceeds the interest rate (g > r)**. India's favourable g-r differential is why a 57% debt ratio is manageable.

A country cannot simultaneously have a **fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and independent monetary policy** — India's answer is the middle path: a **managed float with capital-account controls and inflation targeting**, backed by $690 bn of reserves. Mundell-Fleming.

The shift of household savings from **physical assets and gold to financial assets** — demat accounts above 19 crore, SIP inflows above ₹26,000 crore a month. Note the counter-fact: household **net financial savings fell to multi-decade lows** as household debt rose, the sharpest current macro-prudential concern.

Output growth without commensurate employment growth, because growth is concentrated in **capital- and skill-intensive services**. India's transformation is anomalous: labour moved from agriculture to **construction and low-end services**, not to manufacturing — Lewis's model of surplus labour absorption did not run its course.

Growth that is broad-based across sectors, **creates productive employment**, and reduces poverty and inequality — the 11th Five Year Plan's formulation ('faster and more inclusive growth'). Its measurement: not GDP but **MPI, MPCE, Gini, LFPR and the SDG index**.

groups.g: Environment and technology — name the concept

items.d: **Precautionary principle** (lack of scientific certainty is not a reason to postpone action, and the burden shifts to the developer), **polluter pays** (internalising the externality plus restoration cost), **public trust doctrine** (the state holds air, water, forests and the sea as trustee — *M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath*, 1997), **intergenerational equity**, and **sustainable development** as the balancing frame.
items.s: Vellore Citizens (1996) / M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997)

items.d: **Carbon sink** (India's NDC: an additional **2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO₂ equivalent** sink through forest and tree cover by 2030), **carbon intensity** (emissions per unit GDP — the NDC metric, not absolute emissions), **carbon budget**, **carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM)** — the EU levy India calls unilateral and trade-restrictive, hitting steel, aluminium and cement exports, and **net zero versus carbon neutrality versus climate neutrality**.

**Ecological footprint and biocapacity**, **planetary boundaries (Rockström, nine boundaries, six already crossed)**, **tipping points**, **ecosystem services (provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting)** and **payment for ecosystem services** — India's **forest-cover criterion in Finance Commission devolution (10% weight) is the world's largest PES-like fiscal transfer**, an outstanding value addition.

The **9Rs** (refuse, rethink, reduce, reuse, repair, refurbish, remanufacture, repurpose, recycle) and **Extended Producer Responsibility** — the producer bears post-consumer costs, implemented in India through EPR certificates for **plastic, e-waste, battery and tyre waste**. Contrast with the linear **'take-make-dispose'** model.

**Dual-use technology**, **technology denial regimes** (NSG, MTCR, Wassenaar, Australia Group), **critical and emerging technologies**, **strategic autonomy in technology**, **data localisation versus free flow with trust**, **digital sovereignty**, **splinternet**, **algorithmic bias**, **deepfakes and synthetic media**, and **AI alignment**. Pair a term with a live Indian instrument to make the point land.

**Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability ÷ Capacity = Risk** — the formula worth writing out. **Mitigation** (reducing the hazard's impact) versus **preparedness** (readiness to respond); **structural versus non-structural measures**; **Build Back Better**; **resilience**; **early warning to early action**; and the shift the DM Act, 2005 made **from a relief-centric to a preparedness- and mitigation-centric** approach.

**Hybrid warfare**, **grey-zone operations**, **sub-conventional warfare**, **fifth-generation warfare**, **salami slicing**, **string of pearls versus necklace of diamonds**, **two-front war**, **cold start**, **no first use with credible minimum deterrence**, **radicalisation and counter-radicalisation**, **narco-terrorism (Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle)**, and **money laundering: placement, layering, integration**.

items.t: Crop diversification out of a water-guzzling lock-in
items.d: **Punjab's Kharif paddy and the Preservation of Subsoil Water Act, 2009** — the law delayed transplanting to cut evaporation losses, but groundwater still fell; **Haryana's 'Mera Pani Meri Virasat'** paid ₹7,000/acre to shift out of paddy. *Lesson: a price signal (free power + assured MSP procurement) beats a regulation; change the incentive, not the calendar.*

items.t: Millets as a nutrition and climate answer
items.d: **International Year of Millets 2023**, proposed by India — Shree Anna production ~17 MT; Karnataka's organic and millet mission, and Odisha's **Millet Mission** which put ragi into the PDS and mid-day meals. *Lesson: a crop shift succeeds when procurement, PDS inclusion and consumer demand are created together, not when farmers are merely advised.*

items.t: Contract farming done right and wrong
items.d: **PepsiCo's potato programme in Gujarat** and **Sahyadri Farms** show assured buy-back raising incomes; against them, the Punjab tomato and the **Bt cotton seed-price** disputes show the asymmetry of bargaining power. *Lesson: contract farming needs a dispute-resolution mechanism at the SDM level and a registration authority — the design the model Act of 2018 provides and the repealed 2020 law lacked.*

**AgriStack / Krishi-DSS** — a farmer registry, geo-referenced village maps and a crop-sown registry, with digital crop surveys replacing manual patwari records; **Kisan Drone** and **Namo Drone Didi** (15,000 SHG drones). *Lesson: land-record digitisation is the precondition for every credit, insurance and income-support scheme — PM-KISAN's exclusion of tenants is exactly this problem.*

**Tirupur knitwear** (~₹35,000 crore of exports, a zero-liquid-discharge dyeing model forced by NGT orders), **Surat diamonds** (~90% of the world's cut and polished diamonds), **Morbi ceramics** (second largest cluster in the world). *Lesson: MSME competitiveness comes from cluster externalities — common facilities, testing labs, effluent treatment — not from firm-level subsidy.*

**Mobile phone manufacturing** — from importing most handsets in 2014 to producing ~99% of those sold domestically and **exporting over $20 billion**, with Apple's contract manufacturers scaling in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. *Lesson: incentives work where they meet global value-chain relocation (China+1) — but value addition is still only ~20%, so the component ecosystem is the unfinished half.*

**NHAI's InvIT and the TOT (Toll-Operate-Transfer)** model recycling completed highways to fund new ones; **HAM** splitting construction risk 40:60 between government and developer after pure BOT collapsed. *Lesson: the PPP failure of 2010-14 was a risk-allocation failure, which is exactly what the **Kelkar Committee (2015)** said — 'PPP is not a means of borrowing'.*

**Jan Dhan** — 55 crore accounts, 56% held by women, average balance risen from near-zero to ~₹4,500, with overdraft and RuPay insurance attached. *Lesson: an account is infrastructure, not an outcome — usage came only when DBT, PMJJBY/PMSBY and UPI gave the account a reason to exist.*

**Essar Steel** — resolved under the IBC with ArcelorMittal paying ₹42,000 crore, and the Supreme Court affirming the **primacy of the Committee of Creditors' commercial wisdom**. Against it, the delays beyond the 330-day limit and the ~31% average recovery. *Lesson: the IBC changed debtor behaviour more through the threat of losing control (Section 29A) than through recovery rates.*

**Bhadla Solar Park, Rajasthan (2,245 MW)** and the **Pavagada park, Karnataka** built on a land-lease model that paid farmers rent rather than acquiring land; India's solar tariffs fell from ₹10.95/unit (2010) to about **₹2.4-2.6/unit**. *Lesson: reverse auctions plus solar-park land aggregation collapsed the cost curve — the model now being tried for storage and offshore wind.*

**Delhi's winter smog** — stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana, vehicular and construction dust, and thermal plants, with **GRAP** as the emergency response and the **CAQM** as the statutory airshed regulator across five states. *Lesson: pollution is an airshed problem and cannot be governed within municipal or state boundaries — the CAQM is India's first admission of that in law.*

**Indore, seven-time cleanest city** — 100% source segregation into six streams, a bio-CNG plant of 550 TPD, and a citizen-behaviour campaign; **Alappuzha, Kerala** achieved decentralised composting without a landfill. *Lesson: segregation at source, not treatment capacity, is the binding constraint — a technology-last, behaviour-first sequence.*

**Odisha's Cyclone Phailin (2013)** — 10 lakh evacuated, deaths in double digits against ~10,000 in 1999; sustained through Fani (2019) and later cyclones. *Lesson: early warning is useless without last-mile evacuation capacity — shelters, community volunteers and a colour-coded protocol convert a forecast into saved lives.*

**Joshimath subsidence (2023)** and the **Wayanad landslides (2024)** — construction and tunnelling on fragile Himalayan and Western Ghats slopes, against the Gadgil report's warnings. *Lesson: the disaster was not the rain; it was the exposure and vulnerability created by land-use decisions — carrying capacity studies exist and are ignored.*

**Asiatic lions in Gir: 674 (2020) → 891 (2025)**, and **tigers 1,411 (2006) → 3,682 (2022)** — both achieved with community involvement and dedicated authorities (NTCA). *Lesson: single-species flagship programmes with statutory backing, dedicated funds and independent estimation methods deliver measurable recovery — the model now sought for the Great Indian Bustard and the Gangetic dolphin.*

**Chandrayaan-3 at ~₹615 crore** and **Mangalyaan at ~₹450 crore** — the first successful Mars mission by any country on its maiden attempt, at a fraction of comparable budgets. *Lesson: cost leadership plus indigenous launch capability turned ISRO into a commercial launch provider (NSIL, LVM3 for OneWeb) — capability built for science became export revenue.*

**Aadhaar, UPI, CoWIN and DigiLocker**, presented at the G20 as replicable public goods; **MOSIP** (Modular Open Source Identity Platform) adopted by several countries and UPI live in seven-plus. *Lesson: DPI is layered — identity, payment, data-sharing — and the layering is what makes it reusable, unlike a monolithic government portal.*

**Atal Tunnel (Rohtang, 9.02 km, all-weather access to Lahaul-Spiti)**, **Sela Tunnel (Arunachal)**, and the **Vibrant Villages Programme** (₹4,800 crore for 2,967 border villages) reversing out-migration from the first villages on the frontier. *Lesson: connectivity is deterrence — depopulated border villages are a security vacuum, which is why the programme is framed as security, not welfare.*

**Bodo Accord (2020)**, **Karbi Anglong (2021)**, **Adivasi (2022)** and the **ULFA Accord (2023)**; AFSPA withdrawn from large parts of Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Against them, **Manipur since 2023** shows how ethnic conflict resists the same template. *Lesson: accords work where the demand is autonomy within the constitutional framework; they stall where the conflict is between communities rather than between a group and the state.*

**Over 22 lakh complaints a year** on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal, with digital-arrest scams and mule accounts; the **Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System** and the **1930 helpline** allow freezing of funds in the golden hour. *Lesson: cybercrime is a coordination problem across banks, telecom and police — I4C exists because no single agency can act in the first hour.*

**CPI 4% with a ±2% band**, statutory since 2016; a failure is **three consecutive quarters outside the band**, requiring a written report to the government. Food carries a **45.9% weight** in CPI — which is why headline inflation tracks vegetables more than monetary policy.

**Repo** is the policy rate; the corridor runs from the **SDF (Standing Deposit Facility, repo minus 25 bps)** to the **MSF (repo plus 25 bps)**. **CRR** ~4% (no interest paid) and **SLR** ~18% of NDTL. The **Monetary Policy Committee** decides by majority with the Governor's casting vote.

**GNPA ~2.5%, a multi-decade low**, from 11.2% in 2018; **CRAR ~16-17%** against the Basel III minimum of 11.5% with buffers; provision coverage above 75%. Credit-to-GDP ~56%, well below peers — India is under-banked in credit, not in accounts.

**40% of adjusted net bank credit** — agriculture 18% (with 10% for small and marginal farmers), micro enterprises 7.5%, weaker sections 12%. Shortfalls go to **RIDF with NABARD**, and **PSLCs** allow trading of the obligation.
RBI's index rose from **43.4 (2017) to ~64.2** — access, usage and quality, with quality the weakest sub-index. Jan Dhan: **55 crore accounts, 56% women, ~₹2.6 lakh crore deposits**.

Insurance penetration **~3.7% of GDP**, having fallen, against a world average near 7%; life dominates. **NPS + APY** together have over 8 crore subscribers with AUM above ₹14 lakh crore. IRDAI's target is **'Insurance for All by 2047'**.

The **new PSE policy (2021)** limits the state to **four strategic sectors with a bare minimum presence** and full exit elsewhere. **LIC's IPO (2022)** was India's largest; **Air India's** sale to Tata (2021) the first successful privatisation of a major PSU in two decades. **DIPAM** handles both disinvestment and the **National Monetisation Pipeline**.

**CGST + SGST** on intra-state and **IGST** on inter-state supply; the **GST Council (Art. 279A)** votes with the Centre at one-third and states at two-thirds, decisions by three-fourths. Excluded from GST: **petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF, electricity and alcohol for human consumption** — the unfinished agenda.

GST registrations rose from **65 lakh at launch to ~1.5 crore**; income tax returns filed crossed **8 crore**; **faceless assessment and appeals** removed the assessee-officer interface. Direct:indirect ratio ~**57:43**, a progressivity improvement.

External debt ~**19% of GDP**, with short-term debt a modest share; reserves ~**$690 bn** covering about 11 months of imports and well above the Guidotti-Greenspan rule. India's vulnerability is not solvency but **oil-price and capital-flow volatility**.

groups.g: Environment, energy and security — one figure per line

items.d: Solar ~**110 GW**, wind ~**51 GW**, large hydro ~47 GW, biomass ~11 GW, small hydro ~5 GW, nuclear ~8.7 GW. Solar's cost fell from **₹10.95/unit (2010) to ~₹2.4-2.6/unit** — the fastest cost decline of any Indian infrastructure input.

Domestic production crossed **1 billion tonnes**; coal is ~48% of installed capacity but **~70-74% of generation**, because renewables have low capacity utilisation. India has committed to a **phase-down, not a phase-out** — the wording India secured at Glasgow.

**~8.7 GW installed, target 100 GW by 2047**; the **three-stage programme** (PHWR → fast breeder → thorium) with **Kalpakkam's PFBR** at the threshold of stage two; **Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010's Section 17(b)** supplier liability is the barrier to imports, and amendments to it and to the Atomic Energy Act were announced in Budget 2025-26.

Forest and tree cover **24.62% (ISFR 2021) → 25.17% (ISFR 2023)** against the **33% National Forest Policy 1988 target**; the increase is largely in **open forest and plantations**, while **very dense forest and North-Eastern cover have declined** — always state the composition, not just the total.

Per capita availability **1,486 m³ (2021) → ~1,367 by 2031**; below 1,700 is 'stressed', below 1,000 'scarce'. India has **18% of the world's population and 4% of its freshwater**, and agriculture takes **78-80%** of it.

India's NAAQS for **PM2.5 is 40 µg/m³ annual** against the **WHO guideline of 5**; the **NCAP** targets a **40% reduction by 2025-26** in 131 non-attainment cities. Air pollution is linked to over **1.6 million deaths a year** in India (Lancet/GBD estimates).

**Kunming-Montreal GBF (2022)** — **30x30**: 30% of terrestrial and marine areas conserved by 2030, restoration of 30% of degraded ecosystems, and **$200 bn a year** in biodiversity finance. India's protected-area coverage is ~5.3% of land, so the gap is large; **OECMs (other effective area-based conservation measures)** are how India intends to count community-conserved areas.

Budget **₹6.81 lakh crore (FY26)**, ~13% of the union budget and ~1.9% of GDP; **production ₹1.51 lakh crore**, **exports ₹23,622 crore** to 100+ countries; **75% of the capital procurement budget reserved for domestic industry**; five positive indigenisation lists covering 500+ items. India remains among the world's top two arms importers.

**LWE-affected districts 126 (2010) → 38 (2024)**, target to end LWE by **31 March 2026**; **CAPFs ~10 lakh personnel**; **police-population ratio ~155 per lakh** against the **UN norm of 222**; **police vacancy ~20-22%**; and **women are ~12% of the police force**, against the 33% many states have declared as policy.

**22+ lakh complaints a year** on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal; **NCRB recorded 65,893 cybercrime cases (2022)**; CERT-In's 2022 directions require reporting of specified incidents within **six hours**; India's **Global Cybersecurity Index** score is 98.49 (Tier 1).

groups.g: Instruments and bodies — one line each

items.d: **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices** — an advisory body (not statutory) recommending MSP for 22 crops on the basis of **A2, A2+FL and C2** cost concepts, demand-supply, price trends, terms of trade and the likely effect on consumers.

**Food Corporation of India (1965)** — procurement, storage, movement and distribution; buffer stock and strategic reserve norms are fixed quarterly, and stocks have run far above them, at a substantial carrying cost. **Decentralised procurement** by states is the reform direction.

**1982**, on the **Sivaraman Committee's** recommendation — refinance for rural credit, supervision of RRBs and cooperative banks, the **RIDF**, and the **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (1992)**, the world's largest microfinance programme.

**SEBI (1992)** — protection of investors, regulation of markets, and the LODR framework. **CCI (Competition Act, 2002)** — anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance and combinations, with the **2023 amendment** adding a **deal-value threshold** for digital-market acquisitions and settlement/commitment provisions. **IBBI** — the IBC's regulator.

**TRAI (1997)** with **TDSAT** as its appellate tribunal; the **Telecommunications Act, 2023** replaced the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 — administrative assignment of satellite spectrum, a new right-of-way regime, and interception provisions that have drawn privacy criticism.

**Bureau of Energy Efficiency** under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 — **star labelling**, the **Energy Conservation Building Code**, **PAT (Perform, Achieve and Trade)** with ESCerts, and now the **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme**. UJALA distributed 37 crore LED bulbs, cutting peak demand measurably.

**IN-SPACe** (single-window authorisation and promotion of private players), **NSIL** (the commercial arm), **Department of Space** and the **Indian Space Policy 2023**, which defined the roles and opened end-to-end activity to non-government entities.

**PLFS** (employment, now monthly), **HCES** (consumption, reset the CPI basket), **NFHS** (health), **NSS AIDIS** (debt and investment), **Situation Assessment Survey** (farmer incomes), **ASI** (industry), **IIP and CPI/WPI**, and the **base-year revision** of the GDP series. Quoting the right survey for the right number is itself a scoring habit.

sections.h: Thinkers — The Idea in One Line

items.d: **'The unexamined life is not worth living'** — virtue is knowledge, and wrongdoing arises from ignorance. The **Socratic method** of questioning is the model for probing one's own assumptions in a dilemma.

The **Theory of Forms** and the **philosopher-king** — justice is each part of the soul and of the state performing its proper function. *The Republic*'s 'ship of state' and the **Ring of Gyges** thought experiment (would you be just if you were invisible?) is a ready-made integrity test.

**Virtue ethics** — virtue is a **habit (hexis)** acquired by practice, lying in the **golden mean** between excess and deficiency (courage between rashness and cowardice). The end is **eudaimonia** (flourishing), and **phronesis (practical wisdom)** is the virtue that tells you which mean applies here. The best framework for 'character is formed, not declared'.

**Deontology** — act only on that maxim you can will to be a **universal law** (the Categorical Imperative), and treat humanity **always as an end, never merely as a means**. Duty for duty's sake; consequences are morally irrelevant. Strength: it protects rights absolutely. Weakness: it cannot resolve a conflict of two duties, and forbids lying even to a murderer at the door.
items.s: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

items.d: **Utilitarianism** — the greatest happiness of the greatest number. **Bentham's** felicific calculus is quantitative ('pushpin is as good as poetry'); **Mill** added the qualitative distinction ('better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied') and the **harm principle** in *On Liberty*. Weakness: it can justify sacrificing a minority for aggregate welfare — which is the standard objection to a purely cost-benefit administrative decision.

**Justice as fairness** — principles chosen behind a **veil of ignorance** in the original position: (i) equal basic liberties, (ii) fair equality of opportunity, and (iii) the **difference principle**, permitting inequality only if it benefits the least advantaged. The philosophical charter of affirmative action and of a welfare state.

**Capability approach** — evaluate a society by the **real freedoms (capabilities) people have to do and be what they value**, not by resources or utility. Sen's *The Idea of Justice* prefers **comparative assessments (niti and nyaya)** over a perfect institutional blueprint; Nussbaum listed **ten central capabilities**. The intellectual base of the HDI.

**The banality of evil** — from the Eichmann trial: great atrocity is committed not by monsters but by ordinary officials who **stop thinking** and simply execute procedure. The single most powerful citation for bureaucratic moral responsibility and against the 'I was only following orders' defence.

**Kohlberg's six stages in three levels** — pre-conventional (punishment, self-interest), conventional (conformity, law and order), post-conventional (social contract, universal ethical principles). **Carol Gilligan's** critique: the model is male-coded; women reason through an **ethics of care and relationship**, not abstract justice. Pair the two whenever moral development is the question.

**Milgram (obedience)** — most subjects administered what they believed were lethal shocks when instructed by an authority; **Zimbardo (Stanford prison)** — situational roles corrupt behaviour rapidly; **Asch (conformity)** — people deny the evidence of their own eyes to match a group. The three experiments together are the empirical case for **institutional safeguards over individual virtue**.

**Satya and ahimsa** — truth is the end and non-violence the means, and **means and ends are inseparable ('the means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree')**. **Trusteeship** — wealth is held in trust for society; **Sarvodaya** — the welfare of all; the **seven social sins**; and the **talisman** as the test of every administrative decision.

**'Educate, Agitate, Organise'** — and the trinity of **liberty, equality and fraternity**, with **fraternity as the hardest and most essential**, since without it liberty and equality remain 'a coat of paint'. Constitutional morality must be cultivated. His ethics is institutional: rights are meaningless without the social conditions that make them exercisable.

**'In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness'** — the ruler's dharma is **yogakshema** (welfare and security), pursued through **danda (the rod of governance)** applied with proportion. Also the **saptanga** theory of the state and an early theory of **administrative accountability, surveillance and corruption** ('just as it is impossible not to taste honey placed on the tongue, so it is impossible for a government servant not to eat up a bit of the king's revenue').

The **Tirukkural** — aram (virtue), porul (wealth) and inbam (love); a just sceptre sustains the world, and **'the wealth that comes without a fault is both virtue and happiness'**. High-value because it lets you anchor an ethics answer in an Indian, non-Sanskritic and non-Western source.

**Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path**, with **right livelihood, right speech and right action** directly usable in administrative ethics; the **middle path** as the framework for balance. Jainism: **anekantavada** (the many-sidedness of truth, the philosophical basis of tolerance and of hearing all stakeholders), **syadvada**, and **aparigraha** (non-possession).

**Nishkama karma** — action performed as duty without attachment to its fruit; **svadharma** — one's own duty performed imperfectly is better than another's performed well; and the recognition that a **dilemma is often between two rights, not right and wrong** (Arjuna's dilemma is exactly that). The cleanest Indian frame for 'duty in the face of personal cost'.

**Vivekananda** — 'they alone live who live for others'; **daridra narayana** — service to the poor as worship, and the ideal of **practical Vedanta**. **Tagore** — freedom of the mind, education as the drawing out of the whole person, and his critique of nationalism as 'organised selfishness' when it overrides the human.

items.t: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya and Sri Aurobindo
items.d: **Integral Humanism** — the individual has body, mind, intellect and soul, and development must address all four; **antyodaya**, the rise of the last person, as the measure. **Aurobindo** — the spiritual evolution of consciousness, and the idea that political freedom is only the first step to a fuller human freedom.

A **dilemma** is a choice between **two rights** (loyalty to the institution versus transparency to the public); a **temptation** is a choice between **right and wrong** dressed up as a dilemma. Naming which one the case is — and refusing to treat a temptation as a dilemma — is the single highest-scoring move in a Section B answer.

**Truth versus loyalty · individual versus community · short term versus long term · justice versus mercy**. Kidder's three resolution principles: **ends-based (utilitarian), rule-based (Kantian) and care-based (do as you would be done by)**. Naming the paradigm converts a narrative answer into an analytical one.
items.s: Rushworth Kidder, How Good People Make Tough Choices

items.d: A situation where a public servant's **private interest could improperly influence** the discharge of official duty — actual, apparent or potential. The remedy sequence is **disclose → recuse → divest**, and 'apparent' matters as much as 'actual' because public trust turns on perception.

**Integrity** is the alignment of conduct with values even when unobserved; **probity** adds the procedural dimension — uprightness in the use of public funds and authority. The Second ARC's **'Ethics in Governance'** report is the standard citation; the **Nolan Committee's Seven Principles of Public Life** (selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership) are the standard list.

**Moral courage** is acting on conviction despite risk of loss — distinct from physical courage. **Moral injury** is the lasting damage from being made to act against one's own moral code, or from witnessing it without being able to prevent it — the honest name for what long service under pressure does to an officer.

**Normative drift** — small deviations become the new normal because each is individually trivial; **ethical fading** — the moral dimension of a decision disappears from view once it is framed as a technical, legal or financial problem. Both explain how honest institutions decay without any single act of corruption.

Doing only what the rule strictly requires — 'it is not illegal' as the whole of the answer. The public servant's obligation runs to the **spirit of the rule and the public interest**, not the letter alone; the legal floor is a floor, not a ceiling.

**Relativism** — moral judgements are valid only within a culture; **absolutism** — some acts are wrong regardless of context. The workable position for a civil servant is **constitutional universalism**: the Constitution's values supply a non-negotiable floor while permitting contextual judgement above it.

**Goleman's five components** — self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill. In administration: empathy makes grievance redress meaningful, self-regulation prevents escalation in a crowd situation, and self-awareness is what makes conflict-of-interest disclosure possible at all.

**ABC model — Affective (feeling), Behavioural (action tendency), Cognitive (belief)**; attitudes are changed through persuasion (**Elaboration Likelihood Model — central and peripheral routes**), by resolving **cognitive dissonance (Festinger)**, or through contact. Applied use: Swachh Bharat and Beti Bachao are **attitude-change programmes**, which is why behavioural nudges outperformed construction targets.

**Thaler and Sunstein** — a nudge alters behaviour predictably **without forbidding options or significantly changing incentives**. Indian instances: the **'Give It Up' LPG subsidy campaign**, default enrolment in Atal Pension, the Economic Survey 2018-19's chapter on **'Nudge: from BBBP to BADLAV'**, and the toilet-usage campaigns.

Internal versus external disclosure; the ethical test is **the gravity of the wrong, the exhaustion of internal channels, the reliability of the evidence, and proportionality**. India's **Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 has never been brought into force** — the reason **Satyendra Dubey (NHAI, 2003)** and **Manjunath Shanmugam (IOC, 2005)** are cited as the cost of that gap.

**Responsibility** is the obligation to perform; **accountability** is the obligation to answer for performance to someone with the power to sanction. The **'many hands' problem** — where everyone is responsible, no one is accountable — is why file-noting, recorded oral instructions and single-point ownership matter.

The public servant holds authority and resources **in trust for the citizen**, not as owner — the duty of loyalty and the duty of care. It converts 'discretion' from a personal privilege into a trust obligation, and is the cleanest justification for recusal, disclosure and the public-trust doctrine.

groups.g: Ethics in governance and public service

items.d: **Integrity, impartiality, non-partisanship, objectivity, dedication to public service, empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections** — the values the Second ARC recommended be given statutory form in a **Public Services Bill**, and which the **draft Public Service Code** lists. Add **anonymity and political neutrality** from the Westminster tradition.

items.t: Codes of conduct and codes of ethics
items.d: A **code of conduct** is prescriptive and enumerative — the **All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968** and the **CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964**: no acceptance of gifts beyond limits, prior sanction for acquiring property, restrictions on criticism of government, no participation in politics. A **code of ethics** is aspirational and value-based. India is **conduct-rule heavy and ethics-code light** — the Second ARC's core criticism.

**CVC (statutory, 2003)**, **CBI (DSPE Act, 1946)**, **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**, **PC Act, 1988 (amended 2018)**, **RTI Act, 2005**, **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002**, the **Benami Transactions Act**, **Citizens' Charters**, **social audit**, and the **Integrity Pact** (a Transparency International instrument) used in defence and large public procurement.

**Petty versus grand**; **collusive versus coercive** (collusive is more damaging because there is no complainant); **extortionary**; **quid pro quo versus 'speed money'**; **state capture**; and the distinction between **corruption of process and corruption of outcome**. The Second ARC's phrase — corruption is **'a low-risk, high-reward activity'** — states the incentive problem in one line.

**Corporate governance** (Kotak Committee, SEBI LODR, independent directors, related-party transactions); **CSR under Section 135** — India as the first country to mandate it; **ESG reporting (BRSR)**; and **professional ethics** — the distinction between the **client model, the agency model and the fiduciary model** of the professional's obligation.

**Algorithmic bias and explainability**, **surveillance and the proportionality test from *Puttaswamy***, **informed consent and data minimisation under the DPDP Act**, **deepfakes and synthetic media**, **the digital divide as an exclusion risk in DBT authentication**, and the **precautionary principle applied to AI**. India's **Responsible AI principles (NITI Aayog, 2021)**: safety and reliability, equality, inclusivity and non-discrimination, privacy and security, transparency, accountability, and protection of positive human values.
items.s: NITI Aayog, Responsible AI for All

items.d: **Anthropocentrism** (nature as instrument) versus **biocentrism/ecocentrism** (intrinsic worth of all life — the basis of granting rights to rivers, as the Uttarakhand HC did for the Ganga and Yamuna in 2017); **deep ecology (Arne Naess)**; **intergenerational equity**; and Gandhi's **'enough for every man's need, not every man's greed'**. The **Chipko** and **Bishnoi** traditions supply the Indian instances.

**Common but differentiated responsibilities**, the ethics of **climate finance and loss and damage**, **vaccine equity** (India's Vaccine Maitri, 300+ million doses to 100+ countries), **humanitarian intervention versus sovereignty (R2P)**, and **ethics in international trade** — TRIPS flexibilities and compulsory licensing (India's *Natco v. Bayer* licence for Nexavar, 2012) as the balance between patent rights and the right to health.

sections.h: The Exemplar Bank — The Act, Then the Value

items.d: As Chief Election Commissioner (1990-96) he enforced the **Model Code of Conduct**, introduced voter ID cards and expenditure monitoring, and postponed elections where the machinery was compromised. **Value: institutional courage — using existing powers fully rather than waiting for new ones.**

Delivered the Konkan Railway and the **Delhi Metro ahead of schedule and within budget**, and resigned publicly owning a crane collapse. **Value: accountability without being asked, and the demonstration that a public agency can match private-sector delivery.**

IAS officer who built the **100 km 'People's Road' in Tousem, Manipur** through crowdfunding and community labour when no budget existed. **Value: resourcefulness and mobilisation of social capital where the administrative machinery has no answer.**

Dubey (**NHAI, 2003**) exposed corruption in the Golden Quadrilateral and was murdered after his identity was leaked from the PMO; Manjunath (**IOC, 2005**) was killed for sealing petrol pumps selling adulterated fuel. **Value: the price of integrity without institutional protection — the standing argument for operationalising the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.**

Khemka — **50+ transfers in a career of about 30 years** after cancelling a land mutation; Chaturvedi — CVO at AIIMS, awarded the **Magsaysay (2015)** for anti-corruption work, repeatedly stripped of charge. **Value: integrity has a career cost, which is precisely why fixed tenure (T.S.R. Subramanian, 2013) is a systemic rather than a personal remedy.**

Suspended as SDM in Gautam Budh Nagar after acting against illegal sand mining. **Value: the collision between local political economy and the rule of law — and the reason the Civil Services Board and written orders matter more than exhortations to be brave.**

As IG (Prisons) at **Tihar** she introduced Vipassana meditation, literacy and grievance boxes for inmates — the reforms that won the **Magsaysay (1994)**. **Value: reformative justice and the recognition of the prisoner as a rights-bearing person.**

**S.R. Sankaran** — 'the people's IAS officer', architect of the **Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976** and of SC/ST welfare in Andhra; **Aruna Sundararajan** (Akshaya, Kerala's first e-literacy project); **Rajni Sekhri Sibal**, who protected a merit list under pressure; **Smita Sabharwal, Prashant Nair (Kudumbashree/Compassionate Kozhikode)**. **Value: the district officer's discretion, used for the last citizen rather than the loudest one.**

**Rajendra Bhatt and the Bhilwara model (COVID-19)** — ruthless containment, house-to-house screening and a district-level ring-fence that WHO cited; **Odisha's cyclone evacuations under successive Special Relief Commissioners**; **Kerala's 2018 flood response** with crowdsourced rescue coordination. **Value: decisiveness under uncertainty, and the willingness to act on incomplete information rather than wait for perfect authority.**

Left the IAS to organise the **jan sunwai** movement in Rajasthan, where muster rolls and bills were read aloud in the village square — producing the **RTI Act, 2005**. **Value: transparency as a demand from below, and the conversion of a local practice into a national statute.**

Organised self-employed women — vendors, home-based workers, waste-pickers — into a union and a cooperative bank (1972). **Value: dignity of informal labour, and the insight that the poor need organisation before they need charity.**

**Operation Flood** and Amul — turned dairying into a farmer-owned cooperative and made India the world's largest milk producer. **Value: institution-building that transfers value to the producer, and the refusal of a technocrat to take the commercial spoils of his own model.**

**Sulabh International** — twin-pit toilets and the rehabilitation of manual scavengers, treating sanitation as a question of caste dignity, not plumbing. **Value: technology chosen for its social consequence.**

items.t: Bunker Roy and the Barefoot College
items.d: Trained rural, often illiterate, grandmothers as **solar engineers** — in India and across Africa. **Value: capability, not credential — the capability approach in practice.**

**Chipko (Gaura Devi, Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt)**; **Rajendra Singh's** johad revival (Stockholm Water Prize); **Jadav Payeng, the 'Forest Man of India'**, who planted a 1,300-acre forest on a Brahmaputra sandbar; **Saalumarada Thimmakka**. **Value: individual stewardship of a commons that no law protected.**

**ISRO** — frugal engineering and mission ownership; **the Election Commission** — MCC enforcement; **the Supreme Court's PIL jurisdiction**; **NDMA and Odisha's OSDMA** — zero-casualty evacuation; **Kerala's Kudumbashree** — women's collective governance. **Value: ethics is finally an institutional property, not just a personal one — good people in bad systems get worn down.**

**Bhopal (1984)** — regulatory capture, absent liability and a settlement of $470 million against the actual toll; **the 2G and coal allocations** — discretion without transparent method; **Vyapam and the paper-leak cases** — the collapse of examination integrity; **manual scavenging deaths** despite two prohibiting statutes. **Value: an answer that names a failure and its structural cause reads as honest analysis, not cynicism.**

"Integrity is doing the right thing even when no one is watching." — C.S. Lewis. Pair with **"Character is like a tree and reputation its shadow; the shadow is what we think of it, the tree is the real thing"** (Abraham Lincoln).

"Ability will get you success; character will keep you there." And Gandhi's **seven social sins**: wealth without work, pleasure without conscience, knowledge without character, commerce without morality, science without humanity, worship without sacrifice, and **politics without principle**.
"In matters of conscience, the law of the majority has no place." — Gandhi. And Thoreau: **"Must the citizen ever for a moment resign his conscience to the legislator?"**

Kautilya: **"Just as it is impossible not to taste honey placed on the tongue, so it is impossible for a government servant not to eat up a bit of the king's revenue"** — the earliest statement of the need for audit and surveillance rather than trust alone.
"We can do no great things, only small things with great love." — Mother Teresa. For the case-study conclusion where the officer's remedy is modest but real.
"Nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power." — Lincoln. With Acton's **"power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely."**

"Public office is a public trust" — the American formulation; the Indian version is the **Constitution's oath 'to do right to all manner of people... without fear or favour, affection or ill-will'**, which is worth quoting verbatim in an integrity answer.

Sardar Patel to the Constituent Assembly: the civil servant must have **"independence of expression and fearlessness"** and be free to tell the minister the truth — 'if you do not adopt this course, then do not follow the present Constitution'.

Arendt's **banality of evil** — the Eichmann finding that the worst harm comes from officials who stop thinking. Pair with Milgram's obedience experiments: **the safeguard must be in the system, because the individual conscience is not reliable under authority.**

"The price of greatness is responsibility." — Churchill. And Ambedkar: **"Bhakti in religion may be a road to the salvation of the soul. But in politics, bhakti or hero-worship is a sure road to degradation and to eventual dictatorship."**

groups.g: Justice, compassion and the last person

items.d: "Recall the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen, and ask yourself if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use to him. Will he gain anything by it? Will it restore him to a control over his own life and destiny?" — the test for any administrative decision.
"Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere." — Martin Luther King Jr. And Rawls: **"Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought."**

"A nation should not be judged by how it treats its highest citizens, but its lowest ones." — Mandela. And Humphrey: **"the moral test of government is how it treats those in the dawn of life, the twilight of life, and the shadows of life."**

The Dalai Lama: **"Love and compassion are necessities, not luxuries. Without them, humanity cannot survive."** Use where the case study turns on empathy overriding a procedurally correct but harsh outcome.

Ambedkar: **"We must begin by acknowledging that there is complete absence of two things in Indian society — equality and fraternity"**, and his warning about a life of contradictions between political equality and social and economic inequality.
"The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy." — Martin Luther King Jr.

"The world will not be destroyed by those who do evil, but by those who watch them without doing anything." — attributed to Einstein. And Dante's warning about the hottest places in hell reserved for those who remain neutral in a moral crisis.

"Be the change you wish to see in the world" — and Gandhi's stricter formulation: **"as human beings, our greatness lies not so much in being able to remake the world as in being able to remake ourselves."**

Justice Chandrachud: **"Dissent is the safety valve of democracy"**; and Voltaire's attributed line on defending to the death the right to say it. Useful in answers on protest, free speech and internal disagreement within an organisation.

"First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win" — attributed to Gandhi; and Kalam: **"Dream is not that which you see while sleeping, it is something that does not let you sleep."**

**See**: name the dilemma precisely (which two rights collide), identify every stakeholder and strip the pressure from the facts. **Weigh**: apply four tests — the **legal floor** (what does the rule require at minimum), the **sunlight test** (would this survive publication tomorrow), **reversibility** (would you accept this if you were the affected party), and **precedent** (what does this authorise the next officer to do). **Act**: reject the false binary, then give **Now / Soon / Structural** steps. Conclude by **owning the cost** and naming where reasonable people would differ.

items.t: The four tests, stated for the answer
items.d: **Legal test** — is it lawful, and is lawfulness the whole of the answer? **Publicity/sunlight test** — Kant's universalisability in practical form. **Reversibility** — Rawls's veil of ignorance applied to this case. **Precedent/generalisation** — what happens if every officer does this? Naming the test before applying it is what turns narration into reasoning.

For every case: the **immediate affected person**, the **institution**, the **wider public**, the **subordinate staff whose conduct you are responsible for**, and **future officers who will be bound by your precedent**. Weight is not equal — the ordering rule is **the most vulnerable stakeholder first**, which is Gandhi's talisman operationalised.

Most case studies present two options, both bad. The high-scoring move is to **name the binary as false** and construct a third option — usually by **buying time, escalating in writing, involving an independent third party, or acting on the immediate humanitarian need while starting the formal process**. Then answer why the two given options were rejected.

**Now** — the immediate action within your authority in the next 24 hours (relief, safety, halting the harm). **Soon** — the procedural step (written report, FIR, inquiry, disclosure, recusal). **Structural** — the change that prevents recurrence (SOP, technology, transparency, an institutional check). An answer that stops at 'Now' reads as an emotional response; one that stops at 'Structural' reads as evasion.

Every ethical choice has a price — a delayed project, a personal transfer, a relationship damaged, a lawful order disobeyed. Naming the price you accept, and saying that **reasonable people could disagree here**, distinguishes a mature answer from a self-congratulatory one.

groups.g: Codes, laws and institutions to cite

items.d: **All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968** and **CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964** — integrity and devotion to duty (Rule 3), no gifts beyond prescribed value, prior intimation for property transactions, restriction on private trade and on employment of family members in matters connected with official duty, and **no public criticism of government policy**. The **AIS (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969** govern penalties.

Recommended a **National Ombudsman (Rashtriya Lokayukta)**, **partial state funding of elections**, disqualification on the **framing of charges** for serious offences, an **Office of Ethics Commissioner** for MPs and Ministers, protection of whistleblowers, a **Code of Ethics for ministers, legislators and civil servants**, and the **serving of a false-claim penalty**. The default citation for every governance-ethics question.

**Seven Principles of Public Life** — selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership. Its lasting contribution is the insistence that **holders of public office must be accountable and submit themselves to scrutiny appropriate to their office**.
items.s: Committee on Standards in Public Life, UK

items.d: **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (amended 2018)** — bribe-giving criminalised, **Section 17A prior approval** before any enquiry into an official decision, and the **Section 19** sanction requirement extended to retired officials; **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**; **CVC Act, 2003**; **PMLA, 2002**; **Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016**; **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018**. India ratified **UNCAC in 2011**.

**RTI Act, 2005** — Section 4 proactive disclosure is the ethical heart of the Act, not Section 6; **social audit** (Meghalaya's 2017 Act made it statutory across departments, a national first); **Citizens' Charters** and the **Sevottam** model; **e-procurement and GeM**; the **Integrity Pact** in defence procurement; and **public disclosure of assets** by public servants.

items.t: Ethics for the private and professional sphere
items.d: **Companies Act, 2013** — Section 135 CSR, Section 177 vigil mechanism (whistleblower policy for listed companies), independent directors; **SEBI LODR** and the **Kotak Committee (2017)** on corporate governance; **BRSR** for ESG disclosure; and the professional codes of the **Bar Council, the NMC and ICAI**. Satyam (2009) is the standing Indian corporate-governance failure.

**Mission Karmayogi** — the competency framework (behavioural, functional, domain) with **behavioural competencies that explicitly include integrity and citizen-centricity**; **LBSNAA's** ethics and Sardar Patel Vision; the **Capacity Building Commission**; and the **CVC's Vigilance Awareness Week** with its preventive-vigilance emphasis. Preventive vigilance — systemic improvement — is worth more marks than punitive vigilance.

sections.h: Rapid Recall — Terms, Tests and Dilemmas

items.d: **Values** are what a person or society holds desirable; **morals** are personal beliefs about right and wrong; **ethics** is the systematic reflection on morals and the standards a role imposes. A civil servant's ethics can require setting aside a personal moral preference — that distinction is often the whole answer.

**Intrinsic** — valued for its own sake (dignity, life); **instrumental** — valued as a means (money, efficiency). Kant's 'treat humanity always as an end' is the demand that persons never be reduced to instrumental value.

**Teleological** judges an act by its **consequences** (utilitarianism); **deontological** by its **conformity to duty** (Kant). Virtue ethics asks a third question — **what kind of person does this act make me?**

items.t: Descriptive, normative, meta and applied ethics
items.d: **Descriptive** — what people actually believe; **normative** — what they ought to do; **meta-ethics** — what moral terms mean; **applied** — the resolution of concrete problems (bioethics, administrative ethics, environmental ethics). Naming the branch sharpens a definition question.

Strict adherence to a moral code, especially in the use of public money and authority — 'complete and confirmed integrity'. **Probity in governance** is the Second ARC's framing: it needs both **preventive systems** and **an ethical climate**.

**Objectivity** — decisions on evidence and merit, not preference. **Impartiality** — no favour to any person, party or group. **Non-partisanship** — serving successive governments with equal loyalty. **Neutrality** goes furthest and is the one most contested in a developmental state that requires commitment to social goals.

**Pity** looks down; **sympathy** feels for; **empathy** feels with; **compassion** is empathy plus the will to act. Administrative relevance: empathy without action is sentimentality, and action without empathy is proceduralism.

Putting up with what one disapproves of, out of respect for the other's autonomy — weaker than acceptance and stronger than indifference. In a plural society it is the minimum civic virtue; **Jain anekantavada** supplies the Indian philosophical basis.

The space within which a public servant chooses among lawful options. It is **unavoidable** (rules cannot foresee every case) and **dangerous** (Klitgaard's D). The safeguards are **criteria stated in advance, reasons recorded, and review** — not the abolition of discretion.

The internal moral sense; in administration it is exercised through **dissent recorded on the file, escalation, or resignation** — not through unilateral disobedience of a lawful order. Note the constitutional route: an officer may record disagreement and still implement, which is *Vishaka*-style loyal dissent.

The most common Section B collision. The resolution rule: **loyalty is owed to the office and the Constitution, not to the individual superior** — the oath is 'to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution', not to a person.

The RTI Act's **Section 8 exemptions with a public-interest override** is the statutory resolution: confidentiality is legitimate for a defined class of information and for a defined period, and the burden of justification lies on the one withholding.

The effort of managing one's emotions as part of a job — high in policing, health and grievance-facing roles. Chronic emotional labour without support produces **burnout and compassion fatigue**, which is a management failure, not a personal weakness.

Where insulation from consequences invites risk-taking — bank bailouts, loan waivers, or an officer protected from the results of a bad decision. The counterpart in administration: **accountability without which discretion corrodes**.

**Janis** — a cohesive group suppresses dissent to preserve consensus, producing illusions of invulnerability and unanimity, and the self-appointed 'mindguard'. Remedies: a **devil's advocate**, independent evaluation, and an anonymous channel for objection.

items.t: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
items.d: The more witnesses, the less likely any one intervenes. Its administrative version is the **'many hands' problem**: where a decision passes through many desks, none owns it — which is why file noting, single-point ownership and recorded oral instructions matter.

**Festinger** — the discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs, resolved by changing belief or rationalising behaviour. It explains how an official who takes a first small bribe reconstructs a self-image consistent with it — the mechanism of normative drift.

**Stereotype** — a cognitive generalisation; **prejudice** — the affective attitude; **discrimination** — the behaviour. Interventions must target the right one: contact reduces prejudice, law addresses discrimination, and education alters stereotypes.

**Elaboration Likelihood Model** — the **central route** (argument quality, durable change) versus the **peripheral route** (source attractiveness, quick but fragile). Public-health and sanitation campaigns use both: celebrities for reach, community mobilisers for durability.

**Nudge** — altering choice architecture without coercion; **sludge** — friction that impedes a beneficial choice (the paperwork burden in welfare access); **boost** — building the citizen's own competence rather than steering them. Removing sludge is often more valuable than adding nudges.

**Fiduciary duty**, **independent director**, **related-party transaction**, **vigil mechanism (Section 177)**, **insider trading**, **audit committee**, and **ESG/BRSR reporting**. Satyam (2009) is India's standing failure case; the **Kotak Committee (2017)** the standing reform reference.

**Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice** (Beauchamp and Childress). Indian applications: **informed consent in clinical trials**, the **Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994**, **passive euthanasia and living wills (*Common Cause*, 2018)**, and surrogacy regulation.

**Gilligan and Noddings** — morality grounded in relationship, responsibility and responsiveness rather than abstract rules. Relevant wherever the answer must justify a contextual, person-sensitive decision over a uniformly applied rule.

items.t: Distributive, procedural, restorative and retributive justice
items.d: **Distributive** — who gets what (Rawls); **procedural** — was the process fair (often the stronger driver of perceived legitimacy); **restorative** — repairing the harm and relationship (victim-offender mediation, plea bargaining under the BNSS); **retributive** — proportional punishment.

A superior or minister presses for an unlawful or improper action. **Frame**: legality is the floor; the response ladder is **oral objection → written note recording the reason → escalation to the next authority → seeking a written order** — and implementing a lawful order you disagree with while your dissent stands on the file.

A rule, applied correctly, produces a cruel result for one person. **Frame**: separate the **immediate humanitarian need** (which you can often meet from a discretionary or relief head, or through another agency) from the **precedent** (which you protect by not bending the rule) — and record the case as a reason to amend the rule.

items.t: Conflict of interest in one's own family
items.d: A relative or friend is a party to a decision. **Frame**: **disclose in writing → recuse → have the decision taken by another authority**. Apparent conflict is as damaging as actual; do not rely on your own confidence in your impartiality.

You discover wrongdoing but the internal channel is compromised. **Frame**: gravity of the wrong × reliability of the evidence × exhaustion of internal channels × proportionality of the disclosure. India's **Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 is not in force** — so protecting a subordinate informant is your own responsibility.

A project benefits many and displaces a vulnerable few. **Frame**: utilitarian aggregation is not sufficient — apply **Rawls's difference principle**, the **FRA/PESA consent requirement**, the **LARR Act, 2013's** consent and SIA provisions, and the *Niyamgiri* precedent. The test is whether the displaced are made better off, not merely compensated.

items.t: Speed versus process in a crisis
items.d: Lives are at risk and due process would cost time. **Frame**: act on the **immediate life-safety need under your emergency powers, record the reasons contemporaneously, report at the earliest, and regularise** — the DM Act, 2005 explicitly contemplates this. Never use a crisis to bypass process where delay costs nothing.

You discover petty extortion by field staff who are underpaid and unsupervised. **Frame**: **preventive vigilance first** (transparency of rates, technology-mediated transactions, rotation, grievance line), punitive action against the worst, and honesty about the systemic driver — but never treat the systemic explanation as an excuse.

The right decision will cost you a posting or invite harassment. **Frame**: **own the cost explicitly** in the answer, name the institutional remedies that should have prevented it (fixed tenure, Civil Services Board, written orders), and cite Khemka, Nagpal or Dubey — showing you know the price is real rather than pretending it is not.

sections.h: The Thinker Index — Contribution in One Line

items.d: *The Study of Administration* — founded the discipline; the **politics-administration dichotomy** ('administration lies outside the proper sphere of politics'), the **business-like conception of administration**, and the observation that **'it is getting to be harder to run a constitution than to frame one'**. Advocated comparative study while warning against importing foreign systems wholesale.

*Politics and Administration* — politics is the **expression of the will of the state**, administration its **execution**. Sharpened Wilson's dichotomy into an analytical distinction while conceding that the two functions cannot be assigned to separate organs.
*Introduction to the Study of Public Administration* — the **first textbook**, treating administration as a **unified subject based on management, not law**, with efficiency as its central aim.
*Principles of Public Administration* — asserted that **scientific principles of administration exist and can be discovered**, the high-water mark of the 'principles' phase.

*The Administrative State* (1948) — attacked the fact-value dichotomy and the 'principles' claim, showing that administrative theory carries a **hidden political theory**; administration is a **political process, and efficiency is not a value-free criterion**. Later chaired the **Minnowbrook Conference (1968)** that launched New Public Administration.

'The Science of Public Administration: Three Problems' — a science of administration is obstructed by **values, individual human behaviour, and the social/cultural context**; hence **no universal principles**, and the necessity of comparative study.

The **five paradigms** of the discipline: (1) politics-administration dichotomy 1900-26, (2) principles of administration 1927-37, (3) public administration as political science 1950-70, (4) as management science 1956-70, and (5) **as public administration, 1970 onwards** — the assertion of an autonomous identity.

**Scientific Management** — one best way, time and motion study, scientific selection and training, **functional foremanship**, differential piece-rate, and the **mental revolution** of cooperation between labour and management. Criticism: the worker as an economic animal, 'a physiological machine model'; and Taylorism ignored the informal group entirely.

**14 principles** (division of work, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain with the **gangplank**, esprit de corps, centralisation, etc.) and the **five elements of management: POCCC — planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling**. His contribution is the **top-down administrative theory**, against Taylor's shop-floor view.

*Papers on the Science of Administration* (1937) — **POSDCORB**: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, COordinating, Reporting, Budgeting. Also the **four bases of departmental organisation — purpose, process, persons (clientele) and place**, and the principle of **span of control**. Criticised by Simon as 'proverbs'.

**Ideal-type bureaucracy** — hierarchy, division of labour, written rules, impersonality, recruitment on technical qualification, career service, separation of office from the person. Grounded in **legal-rational authority** (as against traditional and charismatic), and **'technically superior to any other form of organisation'** — yet risking the **'iron cage'** of rationality. Critics: Merton (**trained incapacity, goal displacement, ritualism**), Selznick, Gouldner (**mock, representative and punishment-centred** bureaucracy), Michels (**iron law of oligarchy**), Crozier (the **vicious circle** of bureaucratic dysfunction).

The bridge between classical and human relations — **'power with' rather than 'power over'**, the **law of the situation** (obey the situation, not the person), **integration as the best mode of conflict resolution** (against domination and compromise), and coordination as a **continuous, early, direct-contact and reciprocal-relationship process** (her four principles).

The **Hawthorne experiments (1924-32)** — illumination, relay assembly, mass interviewing and bank wiring room. Findings: **the informal group, social norms and being observed matter more than physical conditions**; the **Hawthorne effect**; and the birth of the **Human Relations school**. Criticism: 'cow sociology', management bias, and neglect of conflict and unions.

**Hierarchy of needs** — physiological, safety, belongingness, esteem, self-actualisation; a satisfied need ceases to motivate. Applied caution: the strict hierarchy does not hold empirically, and in Indian administration security often dominates even at senior levels.

**Theory X and Theory Y** — X assumes an inherent dislike of work requiring coercion and control; Y assumes work is as natural as play and that people exercise self-direction toward objectives to which they are committed. Managerial style is a **self-fulfilling prophecy**.

**Two-factor theory** — **hygiene factors** (pay, policy, supervision, working conditions) remove dissatisfaction but do not motivate; **motivators** (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement) produce satisfaction. Policy corollary: **job enrichment**, not job enlargement.

**Immaturity-maturity theory** — formal organisation with its hierarchy and task specialisation keeps adults in a state of **dependence and passivity**, producing conflict between individual personality and organisational demand; the remedy is **job enlargement, participative leadership and reality-centred leadership**.

**Four systems of management** — exploitative authoritative, benevolent authoritative, consultative and **participative group (System 4)** — with the **linking-pin** concept, where every supervisor is a member of two groups and connects them. System 4 is his prescription.

*Administrative Behavior* (1947) — demolished the 'principles' as **proverbs** (each has an equally plausible opposite); introduced the **fact-value dichotomy**, **bounded rationality**, **satisficing** rather than maximising, the **decision premises** approach, the **zone of acceptance**, and the model of **intelligence → design → choice**. Administration is fundamentally **decision-making**. Nobel Prize, 1978.

*The Functions of the Executive* (1938) — organisation as a **cooperative system**; the **acceptance theory of authority** (authority rests with the subordinate's willingness to accept, within a **zone of indifference**); the executive's three functions — to **maintain communication, secure essential services, and formulate purpose**; and the distinction between **effectiveness (goal attainment) and efficiency (individual satisfaction)**.

**Incrementalism — 'the science of muddling through'** (1959): policy proceeds by successive limited comparisons from the status quo, because comprehensive rationality is impossible; also **'partisan mutual adjustment'** and later **'disjointed incrementalism'**. The realistic counterweight to the rational-comprehensive model.

**Mixed scanning** — combine the rational model's broad scan for fundamental decisions with incrementalism's detailed examination for small ones; a doctor's approach rather than a mechanic's. Also his **compliance typology**: coercive, remunerative and normative power matched to alienative, calculative and moral involvement.

**Yehezkel Dror** — 'optimal model' of policy-making, adding **extra-rational elements (intuition, creativity, judgement)** and meta-policy-making; critic of both incrementalism (conservative bias) and pure rationality. **Geoffrey Vickers** — the 'appreciative system': policy-making is the setting and re-setting of the **norms and standards through which reality is judged**.

**Garbage can model** — in 'organised anarchies' (universities, and much of government), problems, solutions, participants and choice opportunities are dumped into a can and coupled almost randomly; **solutions often chase problems**. The best explanation for why a scheme designed for one purpose is deployed for another.

Founder of the **policy sciences** — the **7-stage decision process (intelligence, promotion, prescription, invocation, application, termination, appraisal)**, and the definition of politics as **'who gets what, when and how'**. Wanted a discipline that was **problem-oriented, contextual and multi-disciplinary**.
